items.body: Rue Oberkampf‘s “Wehmut” is not simply a darker or quieter variation on what the band has done before. The more consequential change is where the music now seems to take its instructions from. Julia de Jouy and Oliver Maier say that although they have recorded much of Rue Oberkampf’s music in a rented cabin in the woods, their more club-oriented work was historically fed by the city. On “Wehmut”, the landscape itself moves into the composition: the Lower Bavarian environment in which they grew up, the Goldsteig trail, the sea between Belgium and Finland, and field recordings that retain the identity of the places where they were captured. That geographical shift coincides with a musical one. Ten years into Rue Oberkampf, the duo feel that much of the current darkwave cycle, including its successive waves and hypes, has already been told. Post-metal and dark folk became important not as genres to imitate, but because of their ability to accumulate tension, physical weight and atmosphere. At the same time, “Wehmut” does not reject the band’s club history. Instead, it seems to open another vocabulary that can eventually be brought back into harder music. The title is equally precise. Rue Oberkampf distinguish “Wehmut” from nostalgia: nostalgia fixes its attention on something irretrievably past, while Wehmut, as they understand it, can be experienced and even enjoyed in the present, carrying longing without requiring loss. That distinction runs through a record concerned with landscape, transience, language and the limited amount of the world any one person can experience. I spoke with Rue Oberkampf about longing for places never visited, why six tracks were enough, using languages as musical materials, what field recordings preserve, the influence of post-metal, the next stage of their live presentation, and why predictability would ultimately be a reason to stop. Wehmut by Rue Oberkampf Rue Oberkampf interview Karo: “Wehmut” has no exact English equivalent; it sits somewhere between melancholy, nostalgia and longing, but none of those words quite contains it. What interested you in building an album around an emotion that becomes less precise the moment you translate it? Does naming a feeling clarify it, or can language also reduce something that is valuable precisely because it remains difficult to define? Rue Oberkampf: Nearly two years ago, we started recording the first fragments of “Wehmut”, and we both had the feeling from the very beginning that this was going to develop in a different direction from the things we had done before. During the creative process, the word “Wehmut” emerged naturally because that was the feeling we both experienced at the time. And yes, we completely agree that the word loses some of its emotional depth when you translate it. But we wanted the title to be a word that expressed something we felt deeply within ourselves. For us, it’s much more about the feeling than the word itself. Wehmut is also closely connected to the region where we were both born and raised. Karo: What I find most intriguing about “Wehmut” is the possibility of missing not only something lost, but something never actually experienced. That almost produces nostalgia without memory. Where does such longing come from for you? Can an imagined place become emotionally as real as a remembered one? Rue Oberkampf: We’re very lucky to have seen many beautiful places around the world. We filmed a video in Patagonia for “Congélation”, experienced temple stays in South Korea, and saw […] landscapes and cities in Japan. During the production of “Wehmut”, we experienced the rough sea on a container ship travelling between Belgium and Finland, and we hiked along the old Goldsteig trail through the Bavarian Forest. Experiences like these stay with you. And as soon as you’re back home, you start missing those places. At the same time, you become aware that there are thousands of other places in the world that you will never see, simply because there isn’t enough time in one life. You can long for something you’ve never even seen. You can imagine its beauty, but you’ll never know what it actually feels like. That’s a beautiful, but also painful, kind of longing. And this is one part of where Wehmut comes from for us. Karo: Four years separate “Wehmut” from “Liebe”, yet the new album consists of only six tracks. Was that concentration deliberate from the beginning, or did the record simply reach a point where adding more would have altered its emotional proportions? How do you recognise when an album has said enough? Rue Oberkampf: You’re right with the second thought. We knew the recording was finished when we felt that every facet of our experience of “Wehmut” had found its place somewhere on the album. Some feelings and emotions don’t necessarily become stronger by repeating them over and over again. Sometimes, saying enough is part of saying something honestly. “Blanc Poney” in particular is a song we’ve loved for years, but we always had the feeling that “Liebe” was the wrong album for it and simply wasn’t the right time to tell that story. So we completely rearranged and re-recorded it from scratch, to bring its soul to a new and more loving home with “Wehmut”. And there’s also a more technical reason: vinyl generally sounds better when you put fewer songs on each side. But that was really more of a nice side effect than a reason for making the album shorter. Karo: The track titles move between English, French, German and Bavarian dialect: “Tonight”, “Come on Moon”, “Blanc Poney”, “Into the Woid”, “Sonne”, “Darkness”. Does changing language also change the emotional temperature of a song for you? Are there ideas that become more intimate, more distant or even more truthful when expressed outside your primary language? Rue Oberkampf: Maybe yes. In fact, we choose languages like we choose instruments or sounds. We close our eyes, listen to what we already have, and eventually words, phrases or even entire sentences come to us very intuitively. We can’t really decide which language we’re going to use before we have the basic structure and sounds of a song. Sometimes the vibe simply seems to call for a certain language. The language becomes part of the sound and atmosphere of the song rather than just a vehicle for the lyrics. Creating art is mostly about listening to what comes up and recognising the diamond ideas hidden within it, and then taking a lot of time to shape and polish those diamonds. Karo: “Into the Woid” is particularly interesting because “Woid” immediately roots the song in a very specific linguistic and geographical landscape. Rue Oberkampf has always carried a cosmopolitan identity, beginning with the French name itself. Was there a conscious desire with “Wehmut” to move away from abstraction and allow actual geography to become part of the project’s identity? Rue Oberkampf: We both grew up in an area of Lower Bavaria with dense, dark forests, small hidden creeks, lots of snow and a lot of rough, untamed nature in general. There are many tiny villages with strong local dialects, surrounded by deep forests. There were times when some of these places could be cut off from civilisation for months during the winter. Even today, you can still feel how deeply this environment has shaped the people who live there. That’s one of the reasons why we’ve recorded almost every Rue Oberkampf album since the beginning in a rented cabin in the woods. But until now, the inspiration for most of our more club-oriented songs came primarily from the city. This time, it was different. We didn’t just record in this area and let the surroundings influence the atmosphere of the recording process. We consciously drew inspiration from the landscape itself, from memories and situations connected to it, and from the particular atmosphere of that region. Karo: The album contains literal traces of places: forest recordings from Buchberger Leite, waves from Kiel, and woodland and owl sounds in “Into the Woid”. A field recording seems documentary, yet the moment it enters a composition it acquires another meaning. Do you regard those sounds as evidence of places you experienced, or as raw material from which an entirely fictional landscape can be constructed? Rue Oberkampf: Actually, the field recordings we use on “Wehmut” are very clearly recognisable as the sounds of the specific places where we recorded them. We didn’t sample them in order to integrate them into melodies or beats, or to create some kind of fictional soundscape. Instead, we wanted to bring the original atmosphere of those places into our songs. In a way, we wanted the music to carry a piece of the actual place with it. The recordings are therefore more like traces or memories of real places than raw musical material. Karo: Post-metal appears among the influences around “Wehmut”, although the record does not simply adopt the obvious vocabulary of that genre. What interested you in it beyond guitars or heaviness? Was it more about duration, accumulation, dynamics, physical weight, or the way tension can be sustained without immediate resolution? Rue Oberkampf: Rue Oberkampf has existed for ten years now, and both of us have the feeling that the story of current darkwave and its many waves and hypes has been told. We felt the need to express something different. Something more organic, mystical and profound. For quite some time, we’ve been listening to many different styles of music, especially post-metal and dark folk. We think that most listeners, apart from perhaps noticing the guitars, wouldn’t necessarily associate “Wehmut” with post-metal. But for us, it was one of the album’s major influences. What interested us wasn’t so much the genre itself, or simply adding heaviness to our sound. It was more the way post-metal can create an atmosphere, build tension and evoke something physical and almost overwhelming. We didn’t want to copy the style. We wanted to take what inspired us, filter it through our own musical language, and make it feel like Rue Oberkampf. Karo: There is an interesting movement through the titles themselves: “Tonight”, the moon, “Sonne”, then finally “Darkness”. I don’t want to impose a narrative that may not be there, but did sequencing the six tracks create an emotional chronology of its own? When you order a record like this, are you constructing a journey or simply finding the most revealing relationship between separate states? Rue Oberkampf: We didn’t do this on purpose, but you’re right: the titles all seem to come from a similar direction. They capture different facets of some of the most exciting and inspiring moments of the “day”: sunrise, sunset and the night. There’s something about these fleeting, hard-to-grasp or dark moments that really resonates with the mystical atmosphere of “Wehmut”. They’re moments that are difficult to hold onto. They appear, change and disappear almost before you’ve had the chance to fully grasp them. We think that quality of transience naturally became part of the album. Karo: You end the album description with the invitation to “be wehmütig with us”. That turns the listener from an observer into a participant. Is “Wehmut” primarily trying to describe an emotional state, or to induce one? And is there an important difference, for you, between understanding an emotion intellectually and actually being placed inside it by music? Rue Oberkampf: As you can see when you come to our shows, we love experiencing emotions together with the audience. So for us, it’s much more about the experience than about intellectually describing an emotion. We always play our new songs to friends before releasing them to see what other people experience when they listen to them. “Into the Woid” was one of the songs that most of the people who heard it beforehand described as being extremely, or even too, sad, which we actually loved because that was exactly what we wanted to express. In that sense, music can do something that words or explanations can’t: it can put you inside a feeling instead of simply telling you what that feeling is. So yes, for us, “Wehmut” is definitely more about inducing an emotional state than explaining it. Karo: “The Singles 2018-2026” and “Wehmut” arrive only months apart. One release deliberately gathers eight years of Rue Oberkampf’s past, while the other revolves around memory, longing and absence. Did encountering your own catalogue retrospectively change your relationship to those themes, or is artistic memory fundamentally different from personal nostalgia? Rue Oberkampf: With “The Singles 2018-2026”, we’re kind of closing a big chapter in our band’s history. That doesn’t mean we’re going to stop producing club-oriented tracks. But we felt that the next chapter, which opens with the very dark and calm “Wehmut”, needed a clean slate and its own space. As for the connection between the two releases, we think there is an important distinction between nostalgia and Wehmut. To us, nostalgia is always about looking back at something that is over, dwelling on the past, on something that can never come back. There’s a certain helplessness to it. Wehmut feels different. It’s a feeling you can actually embrace and enjoy in the present moment. It’s about longing, but nothing necessarily has to be over or lost. In that sense, Wehmut can even contain a positive impulse towards the future. You can feel the longing without simply looking backwards. Maybe that’s also why “Wehmut” doesn’t feel like an album about the past to us. It’s more about being deeply aware of the need to stay focused on the present and enjoy it to the fullest. Karo: I’ve seen Rue Oberkampf live several times, and at Castle Party this year I was struck again by how much intensity you create through restraint: very little movement can make a gesture suddenly carry enormous weight, while the light alternately reveals and removes you from view. Does “Wehmut” require a different physical or visual language onstage? How do you translate absence, distance and landscape into performance without illustrating them too literally? Rue Oberkampf: Yes, we will definitely change some things onstage, but we won’t suddenly become a completely different band after the release. We will absolutely continue playing songs like “Solitude” or “Deine Augen”. But with the new atmosphere that comes with the “Wehmut” songs, we feel that we can tell even more complete stories onstage, with an exposition, a climax and, eventually, a catastrophe. The only exception so far will be a very special two-day event we’re planning in Leipzig in April 2027. We’re currently working on it together with the local promoter, and the idea is to create two completely different worlds over these two nights. Friday will be dedicated entirely to the dark, atmospheric and almost ritualistic side of “Wehmut”, while Saturday will take things in the opposite direction: harder, faster, harsher and extremely club-oriented. We’re planning special support acts, lighting, video and stage design for both nights, so the two shows will feel less like two concerts and more like two different chapters of the Rue Oberkampf universe. We’re really excited about what this could become. Karo: “Wehmut” brings landscape, acoustic elements and field recordings into a project whose live identity remains intensely electronic and physical. Once these songs begin accumulating their own histories through performance, what do you want them to change about Rue Oberkampf? Has this record opened a territory you already know you want to explore further? Rue Oberkampf: For now, we’ve created only dark and calm songs with this particular vibe. We’re very excited to see what impact this inspiration and these influences will have on future, harder or more club-oriented Rue Oberkampf songs. We already have a lot of ideas for new sounds, instruments and even different singing techniques. In this increasingly digitalised world and the current Zeitgeist that inspired us to create “Wehmut”, there are still so many sources of inspiration and impulses waiting to be translated into new Rue Oberkampf songs. So yes, we think “Wehmut” has opened up a territory that we definitely want to explore further, but we’re not quite sure yet where it will take us. Karo: And to finish by looking forward: after “The Singles 2018-2026”, “Wehmut” and the next cycle of live shows, what feels most important for Rue Oberkampf not to become? Is there a version of the project, musically, visually or creatively, that would feel too comfortable or too predictable, and therefore tell you it is time to change direction again? Rue Oberkampf: We’ve never been the kind of band that recreates “Glycine” twenty times with only minor changes just because it works well on streaming and makes us more predictable for Spotify. The focus of Rue Oberkampf has always been on trying things out, taking risks and experiencing our songs together with our live audience in an emotional way. For us, the magic of playing live comes from seeing how people react when the next song doesn’t simply start the way the previous one ended. We like to surprise people and to create moments where they don’t quite know what’s coming next. That can sometimes be unpredictable and less comfortable, but it creates suspense and turns a concert into a shared journey. We’re personally bored by movies that try to convey just one single feeling for two hours. We have a strong inner drive that keeps us from getting bored and pushes us to always try something new. So if we ever become completely predictable, we’ll probably know that it’s time to stop. About Rue Oberkampf Rue Oberkampf was founded at the end of 2016 in southern Germany by three DJs: Julia de Jouy, Oliver Maier and Damien De-Vir. Young & Cold Records describes the original concept as a collision between the energy of 1980s electronic music and the physical environment of techno-era club culture. The group’s own 2026 retrospective credits De-Vir as a member from 2016 to 2023; the current “Wehmut” writing credits belong to Julia de Jouy and Oliver Maier. Their first substantial release was the six-track “Waveclash” in 2018 on No Emb Blanc, followed by the debut album “Christophe-Philippe” on Young & Cold Records in 2019. The 2020 “Negativraum” release appeared through ant-zen, while the second full-length “Liebe” followed on Young & Cold in 2022. Its material moved between EBM and techno-informed tracks, synthpop and darkwave while continuing the band’s multilingual use of French, German and English. The six-track “Essenz” arrived in November 2024. In July 2026, Rue Oberkampf released “The Singles 2018-2026”, collecting “Eternity”, “Eiszeit”, “Solitude”, “I Won’t Surrender (Brutal Edit)”, “Negativraum”, “Sans Toi”, “Deine Augen” and “Never Stop to Dance”. Its credits explicitly document the earlier trio formation and make the compilation a useful dividing line between that period of the band and what follows. “Wehmut” contains six tracks: “Tonight”, “Come on Moon”, “Blanc Poney”, “Into the Woid”, “Sonne” and “Darkness”. The album is released through Young & Cold Records in October 2026; Bandcamp lists the digital release for 15 October, while the label’s own store gives 16 October. The vinyl is mastered by Eric Van Wonterghem, while Ludwig Maier masters the digital and CD editions. Field recordings include forest sound captured at Buchberger Leite for “Darkness”, waves recorded at Falkensteiner Strand in Kiel for “Sonne”, and Scottish owl and forest recordings from the BBC Sound Library for “Into the Woid”. The artwork and design are by Kinnat Sóley. For Rue Oberkampf, “Wehmut” therefore arrives at an unusually explicit dividing point: ten years into the project, immediately after a retrospective gathering eight years of singles, and at the moment when the duo themselves say they no longer find repetition of the current darkwave vocabulary artistically sufficient. The record does not erase the club-oriented Rue Oberkampf; their own answers make clear that they are already interested in what these quieter, more organic and geographically rooted ideas might do once they are pushed back into harder music.

items._cn_summary: Rue Oberkampf在专辑《Wehmut》中显著偏离了既往的俱乐部导向暗潮路线，将创作根源转向下巴伐利亚的成长环境、Goldsteig徒步路径与比利时至芬兰的海域。野外录音保留地点身份，并引入后金属与暗黑民谣的张力积累和物理重量，同时未放弃舞曲基因，而是拓展出可回馈硬派音乐的词汇。标题“Wehmut”被刻意区分于怀旧，强调一种可在当下体验的怅惘，与专辑对风景、短暂性、语言和世界有限性的思索相呼应。六首曲目以环境采样和器乐层次构建氛围，语言本身也被当作声音素材使用。专辑在暗潮脉络中展现出独特的地理感知与声响构造方法，值得关注。

items.body: Most ingredients are well known, but it’s the ingenuity with which they are married into one homogenous alloy that makes Anemoia not simply a standout IDM piece in terms of production proficiency and storytelling, but an important milestone in the history of modern electronic music in general and, for me, a present and future classic. Sonic royalty draped in mastery Anemoia by Ruxpin   I first “met” Ruxpin in the crevasses of a mixtape given to me by my good friend and techno DJ Katia in Zurich sometime in the late summer of 2005 or 2006. She had quickly become a stalwart for deep musical discovery at a rate that would still beat any music search algorithm today. She was especially passionate about a small niche of Icelandic producers who were little known on the European mainland, but who were presenting a very consistent, high-quality output, spreading their goodness on such acclaimed labels as Mikrolux (an Electrolux sub-label) and Uni and the like. I, on the other hand, being ignorant of Ruxpin, was instantly taken, and the intricate sonic layers made a deep impression on my then-IDM-obsessed self, which was chasing abstruse and more involved electronic tunes that sought to make an effort of transgressing the hyper-abstract polyrhythmic lore that had become so en vogue. This impression was deepened when I decided to spend New Year’s of the same year in Iceland with an old college friend and actually met Jonas, aka Ruxpin, in person at what can only be called one of the most random parties of my lifetime. Jonas instantly struck me as a young man with almost suspicious humility but a very clear, ingenious edge, who could not really be bothered with high acclaim and was instead completely focused on channeling his music from a deeper place. Iceland is a territory of particular wild beauty, but never more so than in the depth of what seemed to me like a winter of prehistoric dimensions. A lot has been said about how environments shape artistic output, and while I agree that this seems to be the case, I don’t think that this holds true to the content of the art, but merely to its form and modality. And Jonas’ music bears testimony to this suspicion. This 13-course meal is meant to be savored in its entirety :: 2003’s Magrathea and Elysium, which followed three years later, are not cold by nature, or bare like the outskirts of Reykjavík, even though a first listen might mislead one into becoming stuck with this impression. While they relate the image of technology-driven sonic narratives and insular grit, there is always a tender spark present. Just as I recall Jonas to be a warm and outspoken true artist who chooses his instruments to support his vision and not to become it, there is an undertone of extreme humaneness and delicate embellishment that sets him apart from the IDM predicament of static technocracy. The sub-genre “melodic IDM,” chosen by a variety of digital platforms to index him, is in my view a deceptive misnomer. To me, a more fitting category reads “emotionally intelligent dance music,” and I would largely award Ruxpin the entire category, as such a combination is as rare as common sense in American politics nowadays. As the news of a new full-length Ruxpin album titled Anemoia stumbled into my inbox, I was not only hit with extreme nostalgia and anticipation, but also met with slight terror. Because, as we all have experienced, many good things of former days have shown a tendency of undoing themselves. But just as Jonas had proven the quote “never meet your heroes” wrong, he also dismantled the suspicion that an IDM career cannot be successfully maintained without the loss of identity and quality over such a long period of time. Anemoia is not only a successful continuation of his lineage; it stands on its very own solid feet. At 13 tracks and just under one hour of runtime, this is no lightweight, but the music presented here defies gravity and weight measurements altogether. As a conceptual thinker, I like to attach my sense of an album around a central image. The one I would choose for Anemoia is that of abstract weightlessness, of a heavy landscape that stands suspended, not only in space but also in time. There is a sense of complementary opposition between heavy rolling beats and lofty pads that pervades all the tracks.   The magician the world needs him to be :: Yet another observation must be made. One that is not specific to Anemoia, but to Ruxpin in general: this is a closed-off, integrated and wholesome oeuvre. Breaking it down into individual tracks and noting their individual ingredients and how they stack up against each other is not only doing it a grave disservice, it’s misunderstanding Ruxpin. This 13-course meal is meant to be savored in its entirety, with only brief interruptions to permit one not to lose themselves completely. But even so, this is a canon of high specificity. It is unlike what Jonas presented before, even if his penmanship is clearly identifiable behind every single one of the clearly intentionally designed sounds. These tracks speak of maturing, of a coming of age, and of a homecoming of an artist who has survived the archetypes of warriorship and martyrdom and who is finally the magician the world needs him to be. There are clear traces of inspiration all over this. Crunchy hip-hop beats and even groovy house chords are spun around delicate arpeggios and staccatos that are well known to the IDM crowd, but in their execution, they seem oddly fresh and renewed, reinterpreted in a form that goes far beyond slinging your drum sounds through a 12-bit sampler or an SP-1200 DAC and calling it a day. No, this is about the conscious use of space and how to fill it. Jonas is a master at filling the canvas without overdoing it, at making density seem empty, at giving gas a weight, and turning time into a volume. While many IDM tracks are burdened by the “all buttons in” obsession, Anemoia remains easy without becoming anemic. Glitches and ratcheting never overtake, but are neatly tucked into a mix that has reached masterclass level. A master at filling the canvas without overdoing it :: Particular mention must be given to what has become a standout sound in his productions: the snare drum, or rather the sophisticated modulation thereof. Snares are difficult sounds that lesser experienced producers treat with a criminal lack of attention. On Anemoia, snares seem to carry much of the load and take on much of the duty usually attributed to the kick drum or entire percussion groups. Ruxpin does so effortlessly, but obviously with very great care, and one has to pay close attention to hear how these sounds take on a life of their own over the course of a track. In line with my sentiment that one should not discuss Anemoia as a collection of tracks but as a closed opus, I cannot identify a favorite. All of it seems relevant to the multi-tiered journey. To the point where I would fear that if one was to do the modern thing and only drag one track into their playlist, they would lose 80% of the essence contained and thin the momentum to a mere trickle. What might be a disadvantage to the modern music consumer seeking a quick fix between heavy compression algorithms and heterogeneous, anonymous track lists is a strong selling point for those interested in listening to bodies of work that are woven around storylines that contain the author’s essence and speak of their obsessive despair in rendering an inner vision into a DAW timeline. Yet none of this is to say that the tracks don’t contain life on their own. On the contrary. Just like any good movie scene must move the plot forward, everything is indeed in its right place, and Anemoia convinces with a very effective way of building, sustaining and eventually dissipating energy within every single track, at the microscopic as well as the macroscopic level. For example, “Seduction,” the entry into the album, as well as the two tracks “Aftermath” and “Setting the Sun” leading out of it, are the only ones that don’t greet the listener with an immediate swell of sizzling beats, but instead rely on signature chord stabs and bubbling pads. And “Pleasure Unit feat. Stafraenn Hakon” anchors the LP in its middle with a decidedly stomping march beat that comes as close to being an earworm as Ruxpin will permit.   A common sphere of universal musical wisdom :: There are moments within the journey that are reminiscent of “documentary braindance” and which evoke Boards of Canada-esque nostalgia, relaying a distinct Ektachrome feel because they hit the human brain in the exact same spot. Perhaps another reason why I was so quick to fall in love with its color palette. In a Jungian sense, this album relies, consciously or not, on the existence of artistic archetypes or mood boards, which it shares with other representatives and which take those attuned to it into similar distant terrains. All of this is much more a testament to Ruxpin’s ability to paint with a variety of synesthetic hues than a reductionist approach that borrows out of lack of originality. Akin to my own perspective on what art is, he seems to carve out of a common sphere of universal musical wisdom, rather than create from clay. Most ingredients are well known, but it’s the ingenuity with which they are married into one homogenous alloy that makes Anemoia not simply a standout IDM piece in terms of production proficiency and storytelling, but an important milestone in the history of modern electronic music in general and, for me, a present and future classic. This is sonic royalty draped in mastery. The eclectic electronic producer Ruxpin is one of the leading figures in Iceland’s contemporary electronic music scene. Widely associated with iconic labels such as n5MD and Elektrolux, Ruxpin has stayed true to his roots while continuously evolving his interpretation of melodic IDM, integrating soul and innovation into his music.Now based in Estonia, the artist was born and raised in Kópavogur, Iceland, and became involved in the electronic music scene at an early age. His first release came when he was just fifteen, followed two years later by his debut album on the Icelandic label Uni Recordings. The album received critical acclaim and caught the attention of German label Elektrolux, where he subsequently released his next four full-length albums. Since 2009, Ruxpin has released his work on Móatún 7, Sound In Silence, Ravekjavik, OMNIDISC, Sun Sea Sky, and n5MD. His latest release, however, comes courtesy of Martin Boulton’s Touched Music label.Anemoia is dedicated to Futuregrapher (RIP). Anemoia is available on Touched Music. [Bandcamp] Anemoia by RuxpinThe post Ruxpin :: Anemoia (Touched Music) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了Ruxpin（Jonas）横跨2003年至后期的多张作品合集，评论者将其描述为技术与叙事高度统一的电子音乐典范。与典型的冰冷IDM不同，作品在技术驱动的声响叙事中始终保留温度与人文质感，精致的音层编织和细节装饰使其超越了静态技术主义的窠臼。评论者追溯了自己在冰岛与艺术家本人的偶然相遇，指出冰岛的极端自然环境并未改变作品的内核，而是塑造了其呈现方式与形态语言。整张专辑被视为一份需要完整品味的十三道菜式套餐，每一轨都承载着从更深层流淌出的创作意图，而非追逐高评价的浮华产物，被视为现代电子音乐史上的里程碑式作品。

items.body: Live in Brooklyn, 1992-2002 opens a decade-long aperture through which sound flees its dates and resumes its unfinished conversation with the present. Guitarist Jeffrey Schanzer and pianist-composer Bernadette Speach turn performance into a social form where individual voices ply dreams that are startlingly alive. The duo began collaborating in Buffalo in 1982, joining free jazz and global traditions to the post-Cagean avant-garde. After moving to Brooklyn two years later, they entered an artist-led culture sustained by collective labor. Schanzer served as president of the Musicians of Brooklyn Initiative, founded by Lester Bowie and Oliver Lake with Cecil Taylor; Speach worked as a producer and organizer. When MOBI closed, the pair co-founded MusicVistas, Inc., presenting concerts at Lafayette Presbyterian Church and the Brooklyn Society for Ethical Culture. The guests of those concerts, generously represented here in a selection spanning two discs, reveal a breadth of talent that includes Bowie and Lake, Wadada Leo Smith, Joseph Jarman, Leroy Jenkins, Mark Dresser, Fred Lonberg-Holm, and Alva Rogers. Yet the album resists becoming a parade of illustrious names. Its deepest subject is relation itself, the difficult art of remaining singular while entering another person’s orbit. The open improvisations expose that ethos, each encounter inventing its laws while obeying the fragile discipline of listening. With Lake on alto saxophone, Schanzer and Speach establish a fractured pulse as the horn slips through apertures between intention and reflex. Calls arrive already altered by their responses as the music sheds one skin, only to discover another consciousness underneath. Dr. David Pleasant’s appearance takes a more tactile route. Schanzer strikes the guitar into an ancestral ambiguity while Speach plucks the piano’s interior with aqueous precision. Pleasant’s flute wanders as a spirit negotiating the burden of embodiment, and percussive impacts press against the music’s transparent membrane until fracture becomes illumination. The improvisation with Dresser descends into darker psychic matter. His arco bass draws a vibrating inquiry from an immeasurable well, while scraped textures worry the border between injury and knowledge. Pizzicato attacks bend ordinary hearing. Another improvisation, with Bowie and cellist Fred Lonberg-Holm, replaces abrasion with guarded tenderness. The musicians circle one another through reverb, protecting the work’s secrets from interpretation’s blunt appetite. Jenkins brings ferocious motion. His violin becomes the charged intelligence of a hive mind, agitating guitar and piano into radiance and unease. Beauty here carries no obligation to console. The composed works give these energies names without containing them. On Bowie’s “The Villager,” piano and guitar form a deep foundation for a trumpet voice at once incisive and grief-stricken. Bowie cuts through self-doubt by uncovering the harder question beneath it: What kind of survival leaves the soul intact? His tone pierces without cruelty, and the duo follows its eastern-facing thread into a region where mourning acquires sinews. Smith’s “Rain Flowers, Vertical Spears and Diamond Sunrays,” stretching beyond 24 minutes, is the collection’s vastest chamber of metamorphosis. His koto extends touch itself, entwining with Schanzer’s guitar until chronology folds in on itself. Speach’s toy piano releases tiny constellations over the full instrument’s historical resume. Smith’s muted trumpet seems peeled from an antique surface, its metallic cry approaching a bowed gong’s resonance. Alva Rogers’s “Foreign Affair” turns the album toward the politics of the body. Over Schanzer and Speach’s lush harmonic ground, the composer moves between speech and song, granting each word a physical contour. Her urban narrative of encounter and self-possession refuses the body’s reduction to currency. Desire becomes sovereign, alert to every mechanism that would classify or discard it. In “Glove Quartet,” Holland Hopson’s soprano saxophone and electronics meet John J.A> Jannone’s circuitry and Schanzer’s aggressive electric guitar. The surfaces grow harder, but lyricism keeps opening hidden doors in the machinery. Jarman’s “Hollows Five: II – Sincere Words. Can’t Compromise or Overpower” offers the most immersive ritual. Bells and bowls summon depth without exoticizing it; piano and guitar locate pressure points within the surrounding network. Jarman’s flute and alto saxophone carry a restless human shade through recurring figures. Brooklyn’s so-called second renaissance took material form. It required rooms, organizers, trust, and the stubborn conviction that art could build forms of civic life unavailable elsewhere. Schanzer and Speach hoped these recordings would transport listeners to that place and time. They accomplish something stranger. The album makes the past responsible to the future, asking whether listening can become a moral practice rather than private consumption. Within these performances, freedom means the exacting effort of making space for another consciousness without furnishing that space in advance. Perhaps the archive ultimately exceeds remembrance and becomes a score for communities that do not yet exist, waiting inside us for the courage to become audible. The post Schanzer/Speach Duo with guests: Live in Brooklyn, 1992-2002 appeared first on Sequenza21.
items._cn_summary: 这张双碟现场录音集跨越1992至2002年，记录了吉他手Jeffrey Schanzer与钢琴家Bernadette Speach在布鲁克林策划的系列音乐会精华。二人1982年起在布法罗合作，将自由爵士、世界音乐传统与后凯奇式前卫美学融合，移居布鲁克林后深度参与艺术家自治的演出生态。专辑邀请了Lester Bowie、Oliver Lake、Wadada Leo Smith、Joseph Jarman、Leroy Jenkins等横跨自由爵士与先锋即兴领域的音乐人同台，但核心议题并非名角展示，而是关于'关系'本身——在保持个体独特性的同时进入他人的声音轨道。现场即兴段落展现各场对话的独特法则：Lake的次中音萨克斯制造裂隙般的脉搏，David Pleasant的长笛如游走的精神体，Dresser的拉弦低音潜入幽暗心理地带，Bowie与Lonberg-Holm以克制温柔抵御过度诠释，Jenkins的小提琴则带来蜂巢般的激烈动能。

items._cn_summary: 获奖作品《And I sole ear》以逐一精心制作的电子声响素材与器乐声部相融合，评委指出其结构完整、戏剧性发展成熟，并通过自然合一的内在音响世界提出了深层追问。中桥祐纪的创作体现了电子原声手法在当代管弦乐中的细腻应用，声音素材与乐器音色之间形成紧密对话，而非简单拼贴。作品在整体架构上具有清晰的叙事逻辑，电子音色作为材料而非装饰，服务于作品的精神内核。该奖项以公开演奏会形式评选，侧面印证了作品在演出效果层面的完成度。中桥祐纪的学院背景和国际获奖经历也为其声响探索提供了技术支持，使其在电子与器乐的复合维度中保持了平衡与说服力。

items.body: Of course, this trio is a supergroup, like so many of pianist Vijay Iyer’s latest ensembles. Percussionist Dafnis Prieto may be less well-known, but the now 82-year-old saxophonist and flutist Henry Threadgill is all the more so. Despite his age, he has been more productive and acclaimed than ever. He won the Pulitzer Prize for his most important work of the past 15 years, In for a Penny, In for a Pound (Zooid; 2015). It’s possibly the most consistent realization of Threadgill’s compositional system, in which he works with predetermined interval sequences that provide the musicians with a harmonic and melodic framework within which they are also expected to improvise - that is, improvisation itself becomes part of a highly complex composition. What’s fascinating about this is that the music initially seems almost chaotic, but is in fact organized with extraordinary precision. As intellectually fascinating as this music is on the one hand, it has also faced criticism on the other hand, that the whole thing is too contrived and too lifeless, too close to new classical avant-garde music. That kind of criticism can certainly not applied to “Fifteen”. The album title refers to the number of years that have passed since this trio first came together at a benefit event for the New York Jazz Gallery. Here, all three compose and improvise; recurring melodic patterns are readily - even eagerly - embraced, bringing the music closer to mainstream jazz than to free jazz. This is primarily due to Dafnis Prieto’s Cuban influences and his light, elastic groove, which remains free and almost impossible to count. This is perhaps most clearly evident in “I Want a Map”, which comes across more like a rock song, with Threadgill’s saxophone initially taking up the melody, which is developed by the piano and built up relatively straightforwardly by the drums to a crescendo. Rarely has Threadgill sounded so accessible; he uses a fair amount of growl, and his clear sound from the Air years is barely recognizable. But he wouldn’t be Henry Threadgill if he didn’t gradually incorporate small atonal elements and offbeat shifts that disrupt the piece’s static structure. Things get significantly wilder on “Fire City“, then. Prieto plays less to the beat. Here, he actually acts more like a free jazz drummer. Iyer, too, plays fewer tonal harmonies, and Threadgill’s sound is indeed clearer and more abstract on this track. The piece is denser, less airy than others on the album, but perhaps that’s precisely what makes it the most exciting, as it gallops off in different directions several times without ever losing its way. The most unusual track is the album’s finale, “On the Way”. Here, the different compositional and improvisational logics stand in direct contrast to one another: Henry Threadgill’s carefully balanced vocabulary meets the rhythmic power and temporal sophistication of Iyer and Prieto, opening up spaces for dense ensemble polyrhythms and incisive solo passages. At times, you can literally tap your foot along - you almost feel like dancing. Who would ever have expected that from an album featuring Henry Threadgill? This is definitely one of the albums that will appear on many year-end charts. Fifteen is available on vinyl, as a CD and as a download. You can listen to it and buy it on Vijay Iyer’s bandcamp site: Fifteen by Henry Threadgill, Vijay Iyer, Dafnis Prieto Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free jazz / avant-garde jazz / experimental / modern composition
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Henry Threadgill、Vijay Iyer与Dafnis Prieto组成的三重奏录制，标题“Fifteen”指三位乐手自初识以来已过去十五年。作品在Threadgill高度复杂的作曲系统与自由即兴之间取得平衡，预设音程序列提供了灵活的旋律与和声框架，听起来近乎混沌却组织精密。与Threadgill早期作品相比，此作更富律动感，尤其得益于Prieto带有古巴音乐根源的轻巧弹性鼓点，使整体氛围比典型自由爵士更贴近主流爵士。《I Want a Map》带有摇滚式的直白推进，随后逐步引入无调性元素打破稳定；《Fire City》则更狂野自由，鼓与钢琴脱离和声常规，呈现密集而不可预测的走向；终曲《On the Way》将Threadgill的精确语汇与Iyer、Prieto的节奏张力并置，在复杂复节奏与独奏段落中开辟出独特空间。整张专辑在严谨结构与即兴活力之间实现了罕见的融合。

items.album: No Longer Lost: David Sylvian’s Gone to Earth at 40
items.tags: experimental electronic jazz world psych prog

items.body: Both soothing and unsettling, David Sylvian's much-overlooked second solo album is as much a forerunner of post rock as more celebrated work by Talk Talk, argues Toby Manning, as he returns to the album four decades on With David Sylvian often dismissed as ‘new age’, his evanescent second solo album, Gone To Earth, might be better remembered if reframed as dream pop or post rock. Jettisoning the few vestiges of rock that remained on his solo debut, 1984’s Brilliant Trees, Sylvian’s Gone To Earth reflected how, in the 80s, popular music, like the workplace, was being unmanned, rock’s dynamics deconstructed. As vocalist and focal point for Japan, Sylvian was a poster boy for this societal shift, a Catford ratcatcher’s son who,... The post No Longer Lost: David Sylvian’s Gone to Earth at 40 appeared first on The Quietus.

items._cn_summary: 《Gone to Earth》是David Sylvian的第二张个人专辑，在四十周年之际被重新审视。乐评指出，这张专辑常被误归为新世纪音乐，实则更接近梦幻流行或后摇滚，甚至被视为后摇滚的先声。专辑摒弃了前作中残存的摇滚元素，将摇滚的动态结构解构，以缥缈的氛围、细腻的声场和克制的情感表达，呼应了八十年代流行音乐去男性化、去中心化的文化转向。Sylvian作为前Japan乐队主唱，在这张作品中展现了从偶像歌手向实验艺术家转型的轨迹。其声音设计兼具安抚性与不安感，在梦幻与暗调之间游走，融合了ambient的绵延、爵士的即兴气质与前卫的编排思维。文章强调这张作品在音乐史上的位置被低估，其跨类型探索与同时期Talk Talk的后期作品同样具有开创性，值得从梦幻流行和后摇滚的脉络中重新聆听与定位。

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Simultaneously posted to my blog (Scott's Song by Song Spotlights) with links for listening and purchasing.Today's album is slightly older than my more recent reviews, but certainly not an old album. Released on December 5 of 2025, "Elliptical Passage" is a collaboration between Barry Cleveland and Robert Rich (no relation to me that I am aware of). According to the press release I have received:Barry Cleveland is an LA-basedcomposer, guitarist, recordist,journalist, and author. His sevenalbums showcase a range of stylesfrom ambient to avant-rock to worldfusion. Cleveland also penned thecult classic book Joe Meek's BoldTechniques, and served as an editorat Guitar Player magazine for 12years. (barrycleveland.com)Robert Rich has released over 60albums across five decades,defining his unique language ofambient electronic music. Richbegan building synthesizers in1976, when he was 13, and laterstudied computer music atStanford's CCRMA whileresearching lucid dreaming. His allnightSleep Concerts have becomelegendary. (robertrich.com)Barry says the album began when he discovered some decade old recordings he had made. While improvised, he felt that the ideas had musical merit, and he contacted Robert Rich about using the recordings as a basis for an album, and he agreed. Recently, Barry reached out to me about reviewing this album, and I agreed. As always, I receive no additional compensation, and I call it like I hear it. As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Album credits:Produced by Barry Cleveland and Robert Rich.Mixed and mastered by Robert Rich.BC: Guitar, pizzicato arpeggione, bass, gongs, bowed cymbals, loopers.RR: Piano, flute, lap steel, percussion, Prophet X, Haken Continuum.All compositions by Barry Cleveland and Robert Rich.Primary guitar figure in "Zero of the Sanctified" derived from a line by Steve Rapetti. Track 1: Tangible Silence (6:55)This fades in with sustained synth chords, and swelling guitar notes. As it progresses, there are some interesting low pitched tones. The music gradually crescendos. There are no noticeable underlying rhythms. This might make a good meditation track. Various tones come in and out of the soundscape. At around 4:20 a flute takes the spotlight and most of the other sounds drop out. Different sounds gradually come back in. This reminds me of the introduction from Led Zeppelin's "In the Light". While this type of track is not in my usual wheelhouse, I can tell you that I enjoyed it and I found it to be well-done.Track 2 - Beckoning Voices (6:26)This one came so smoothly out of the first track, that I initially didn't realize that the track had changed. Once again there are long sustained sounds at first. However, a bass pattern begins to emerge, giving a sense of rhythm and momentum that the first track did not have. The overall sound, however, is still based on long, floating sustained tones. The music on this album, so far, would work as the soundtrack for a movie about space travel. The sounds are quite interesting and engaging. Later in the track, the bass pattern has dropped out, but the melodies are becoming more pronounced, with some subtle rhythms on piano. Intriguing track.Track 3 - Elliptical Passage (8:31)Once again, the transition from one track to another is seamless. A sound that makes me think of a spaceship enters the soundscape. This one feels more ominous than the first two. That said, there are some lighter tones in with the more foreboding ones. At around 3 minutes in, there are reverse recorded guitar sounds. Some harmonics are played in octave unison with a descending bass line after 4 minutes in. At around 6:45 there is a sustained guitar melody that actually reminds me of a melodi in Fleetwood Mac's everywhere. Another point of reference is that some of the sounds just before the eight minute point remind me of ones in Phil Collins' classic "In the Air Tonight". Track 4 - Gathering Stars (12:53)Once again, the transition is seamless. The guitar harmonics float on top of the sustained tones. The slide guitar notes are a recurring feature of the music. Some of the tones remind me of "In the Light" once again. I feel like we are about to "arrive" somewhere at about 8:30. This is becoming more intense as it goes along. The bass notes provide some tension and release. This is less melodic than its predecessor. The last portion has some hopeful sounding brighter tones. Track 5 - Luminous Expanse (10:51)As has been the case throughout, another seamless transition. The title implies sunrise over a wide, open area, And that is what the music implies to me as well as this track emerges. There is a subtle underlying rhythmic pattern on this one. The flute brings an organic touch to the soundscape. At around 6:40, there are some distorted power chords in the mix, but they are not the most prominent part. The guitar chords become more prominent at around 9:30. Track 6 - Zero of the Sanctified (9:30)As this one transitions out of the previous one, there are some clean guitar chords and a bit of smooth lead guitar phrases, but all still very sustained. The guitar is much stronger and more up front than it has been on the other parts of the album. This one is more horror movie soundtrack like than floating through space. The longer it goes on, the more disturbing it gets. The music calms down at around 5:30 and becomes more peaceful. The music begins to fade a bit with about one minute left, then some chime-ey guitar notes close the album out. OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:While electronic, ambient music is not really my favorite subgenre of prog, I can tell that Barry Cleveland and Robert Rich took great care in where every note and sound was placed on the album. The soundscapes are warm and rich. Fans of this genre will love this album. So, while it is not really an album that I will likely return to very often, I must reward the quality of it. I give it a 4 out of 5 stars. Or 80%. Many will rank it higher.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Barry Cleveland与Robert Rich的合作，源于十年前即兴录音的再创作。Cleveland贡献吉他、琶音琴、低音与铜锣等，Rich则负责钢琴、长笛、滑柄吉他及合成器，两人以层叠的长音和缓慢演进的声响结构构建出冥想般的氛围。开篇曲目以持续的合成器和弦与吉他音浪铺陈，随后长笛独白引入变化；第二首从第一首无缝过渡，低音线条带来律动感。整体音乐缺乏明确节拍，更接近漂浮的声响景观，适合专注聆听或氛围背景。乐评人特别提到其音色过渡自然，并联想至Led Zeppelin某首作品的开篇气质，但整体仍属于前卫电子与氛围实验的范畴，展现出两位资深音乐家对声场细节的精准掌控。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — What I find interesting when listening to Mountains is, first, the use of folklore from regions bordering the band's native Finland, as if the depths of Nepal and the Himalayas were leading the way there, and second, how that same folklore lent itself, much like Middle Eastern traditions, to the sinuous, serpentine melodies characteristic of psychedelia; it is as if something ancient from the East were meeting the West to erupt into that invisible form of music. In this way, Hadal Sherpa immerses itself, with a synthesizer backdrop evoking outer space, in populating the soundscape with constellations, featuring guitar solos weaving between rhythm and lead parts, alongside a flute that highlights the desert-like, austere, and climatically violent and aggressive nature of their music. Goat Gaze will amplify these qualities with the captivating spell of a flute that dances over the psychedelic textures like a serpent.Starting with Dark Tides, one can find certain similarities to Hawkwind, yet Eastern time signatures are a constant presence, capitalizing on the sense of confusi�n, a kind of claustrophobia, arising from the relentless repetition of notes that shrink a space which, mere moments earlier, had seemed infinite.Upon listening to Ormus, one might even draw a parallel to John Zorn's Electric Masada, a comparison anchored here by the virtuosity of guitarist Vesa Pasanen. "Return to Farum Azul" breaks a certain stylistic monotony through the inclusion of a choir, lending the track an epic, palatial atmosphere."Mountains" and "Gurbet" resume the cosmic journey, drawing parallels with deserts and mountains, and that ascent into the infinite which serves as the album's central metaphor, with profound stylistic richness, though perhaps with an overly narrow focus on just one facet of that spectrum of possibilities.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑将芬兰乐队对近东及喜马拉雅地区民间音乐的想象融入迷幻摇滚框架，以合成器营造太空质感，吉他独奏穿梭于节奏与主奏之间，长笛声线如蛇般盘旋于迷幻音景之上。专辑借鉴中东传统调式与蛇形旋律走向，使古老东方元素与西方摇滚语汇交汇碰撞。部分曲目呈现霍金威式的太空摇滚气质，同时融入东方节拍带来的重复性压迫感；另一些段落引入合唱与史诗氛围，突破风格单调。吉他演奏展现出高度技巧性，接近实验爵士的前卫路线。整体以山脉为隐喻展开宇宙之旅，风格集中在迷幻与东方融合的一个侧面，虽略显聚焦过窄，但文化跨度与音色实验使其在世界音乐与前卫摇滚交叉领域具有独特价值。

items.body: Tuğçe Şenoğul Atlas self-released There’s precious little information in English about Turkish vocalist Tuğçe Şenoğul. Aside from references to her time as one half of Seni Görmem İmkansız, and a few scattered write-ups about various collabs, it’s hard to find much reliable on the Istanbul-based artist. With that said, her streams on Spotify and Turkish language coverage certainly attest to some degree of popularity in her home country, with her new album Atlas (following from EP of the same name a few years back) demonstrating an intriguing mixture of modern electropop and traditional folk music. How that works in practice is fairly straightforward; on tracks like “Serseri” and “Cennet” Şenoğul mixes smoky, trip-hoppy production with strings, percussion and horns, all blended with a remarkable smoothness that speaks to the overall earthy and organic vibe of the compositions. Not every track relies on the mixture of traditional and electronic instruments – the lovely opener “Kırık Hikaye” is entirely made up of electronic ambiences, while “Bu Gece” is largely a simple piano based composition – their deployment a testament to the more measured and sensuous vibe of the instrumentals. It’s of course easy for the non-Turkish listener to get caught up in the novelty of hearing these sounds and musical approaches brought together, but there’s actually an interesting tension in how complex the arrangements and songwriting performance are, and Şenoğul’s presence as a vocalist. The record is very much at its best when the instrumentation gets out of her way and lets her take all the focus. The title track features a lovely mixture of percussion and some very interesting stringed instruments along with its throbbing electronic pulse, but it’s all about hearing how she slides between each different element, forceful without needing to belt it out or even change the urgency of her delivery. The tracks with a slightly more traditional structure end up being a mixed bag; “Sensin Bunlara Sebep” is a more traditional pop take on Turkish folk but is far less intriguing than the loungey, Collide-esque sounds of “Hatıramızla”, delivered with a reserved but coy wink. While you’ve got a few tracks in the mix like “Aşk Deli” that could fit on a darkwave dancefloor alongside Kite, the real appeal of Atlas lies in its warm, enveloping production and the power of Tuğçe Şenoğul as a performer. Even without knowing a lick about the themes and topics of these songs, she cleanly communicates love, sorrow, loss and resolve, picking her spots to hold back, where she employs her full range, and knowing how each bit of phrasing and inflection effects the whole. Buy it. Atlas by Tuğçe Şenoğul The post Tuğçe Şenoğul, “Atlas” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._genre: electropop / Turkish folk fusion / trip-hop / darkwave
items._cn_summary: 土耳其歌手 Tuğçe Şenoğul 的专辑《Atlas》将现代电子流行与土耳其传统民间音乐融合，呈现出有机而温暖的质感。弦乐、打击乐与铜管被编织进烟雾感的三拍子电子制作中，过渡平滑自然。部分曲目以纯电子氛围或简约钢琴为主，展示了编曲的多样层次。评论特别强调人声表现力——Şenoğul 在复杂编曲中不刻意炫技，仅凭语气的轻重与气息的收放传递悲喜与决绝。专辑在传统结构曲目中表现参差，但在 lounge 风格与 darkwave 舞曲气质的作品中更具吸引力。整体制作温暖而包容，作为土耳其本土独立发行作品，展现了非西方音乐场景中东西方元素交汇的可能性。

items.body: 会期：2026/07/02～2026/07/05 会場：一心寺 南会所［大阪府］ 公式サイト：https://hmp-theater.com/work/kanidenka/ リーディング公演は、「本公演のための試演会」「低予算でも可能な簡易版」と思われがちだ。だが、大がかりな舞台セットや音響、照明、衣装などの演出で色を付けられない分、「声に出して読む」という戯曲の本質が抽出され、戯曲自体の構造がクリアに浮かび上がる。とりわけ、リフレインのリズム感、アンサンブルによる音楽的リズムの増幅、居酒屋のメニューや街中の看板など「演劇の台詞として書かれたものではない言葉」を戯曲に取り込む手法が駆使されている場合、「リーディング」という形式の意義や魅力が際立つ。 リーディング公演『KANIDENKA』は、維新派を主宰した松本雄吉の没後10年を契機とし、大阪を拠点とする劇団、エイチエムピー・シアターカンパニーが企画した。構成・演出は、同カンパニーの俳優で、維新派に一時在籍していた髙安美帆。松本は1970年に「日本維新派」を結成し、1987年に「維新派」と改称した後、1991年の『少年街』にて「ヂャンヂャン☆オペラ」という独自のスタイルを確立した。劇団員自らが巨大な野外劇場を建設・解体し、5拍子や7拍子のリズムに乗せて大阪弁で語るのが特徴である。名称は、活動拠点の大阪にある、通天閣で知られる下町「新世界」にあるジャンジャン横丁から取られている。 1984年初演の『蟹殿下』は、初期の日本維新派時代から独自のスタイルを確立するまでの過渡期にある作品だが、原点といえる要素が多く詰まっている。例えば、「淡路島」「小豆島」「豊島」「直島」と羅列される島の名前が、瀬戸内海から九州南端へと抜け、奄美大島、沖縄島、宮古島、そしてパラオ、ミクロネシア連邦、マーシャル諸島など大日本帝国時代に委任統治領となった南洋諸島を含む島々へと続いていくシーンは、後の代表作『台湾の、灰色の牛が背のびをしたとき』（2010）を既に内包している。戯曲は『維新派・松本雄吉 1946～1970～2016』（‎リトルモア、2018）に収録。 「蟹殿下」と宛名が書かれた巨大な封筒が地面から出現して始まる『蟹殿下』には、明確なストーリーはない。ジャンジャン横丁に迷い込んだ蟹（＝酔っ払った放浪の男）が、「親愛なる路地の殿下へ……」と呼びかける女たちの声に誘われ、飲み屋街から路地を抜けて南港の海まで歩いていく旅が、さまざまな情景や言葉のコラージュとして描かれる。南港フェリーターミナル広場での初演時には、更地に碁盤の目の溝を掘り、その上に板と土をかぶせて再び更地に見えるようにした仮設劇場を建設。作中に頻出する「穴」「マンホール」のように出演者が地中から出入りし、クライマックスではクレーンに吊り下げた巨大な月が昇る演出がなされた。また、ト書きでの情景描写に加え、記録写真を見ると、ふんどし一丁の出演者が金粉ショーを披露するなど、ビジュアル要素の強い上演であったことがわかる。この戯曲を、ビジュアルに頼らずに、俳優の声によってどう立ち上げることができるか。 ［撮影：井上嘉和］ リーディング公演で強く感じたのは、演劇として都市の路上へ眼差しを向けること、そして異なるレンズの使用によって視野や解像度の違いが浮かび上がる点だ。本作では、鳥の目のように俯瞰する視線と、虫のように地べたを這う視線が同居する。「通天閣の向こうがわは？」「ジャンジャン横丁」「ジャンジャン横丁の向こうがわは？」「まちだ胃腸病院」「まちだ胃腸病院の向こうがわは？」「てんのじ村」と続く問答は、娯楽施設、学校、橋、変電所、貯木場と街中のランドマークを点と点でつなぎながら飛び越え、南港フェリー埠頭に着地する。そこから先に広がるのは、淡路島から瀬戸内海を越え、太平洋へと果てしなくつながる島の数々だ。一方、本作のキーワードのひとつが、「蟹」と「亀」という、海を生まれ故郷とし、地べたをのろのろと這う生き物だ。ジャンジャン横丁で酔っ払った男は、路地に迷い込んだ亀を見つけ、「かわいそうになあ、よーし、俺が連れて帰ったる、海まで連れて行ったる、まかしとけ、ジャンジャン横丁案内して、海まで連れて行ったる、（略）ちょっと酔うてはおるけどなあ、海まで行く道はよう知っとんのや」と掌に載せる。社会から「虫けら」のように踏み潰され、除け者にされる存在どうしの人情と、頼りなさや情けなさ。また、ト書きでは終盤、路地を放浪する男たちが体を寄せ合うと、頭の被り物が亀の甲羅に変容し、吹き上がる水しぶきのなか、ゆっくりと海へ向かって歩いていく。 また、路地の点描のシーンでは、「ビール大三八〇エン」「エビフライ三八〇エン」「冷ヤッコ一〇〇エン」といった壁のメニュー、「権利金保証金なし」のアパートの張り紙や街中の看板の文字が読み上げられる。「演劇の台詞」として書かれたものではないが、注文の際、声に出して読まれる言葉。酒や娯楽、宿を探し求めて路上を歩く人々に呼びかける看板の文字。街中には潜在的な演劇の台詞が膨大に存在している。松本の視線は、街を歩きながらそれらを収集し、コラージュする。再開発や観光地化でもう存在しない街並みを、断片的な言葉として収集・保存する、アーカイブとしての戯曲がここに立ち上がる。複数の道が交差する都市の路上はまた、直線的な一筋の道で物語化することへの抵抗ともなる。また、本作は、ヴァルター・ベンヤミンが『パサージュ論』で提示した、近代都市の消費空間をそぞろ歩く「遊歩者」のバリエーション（大阪の下町バージョン）ともいえるだろう。 ［撮影：井上嘉和］ 戯曲ではただの情報や文字の羅列だったものが、複数の声で読まれ、時にアンサンブルとして共鳴することで、立体的な音響として世界が実体的に立ち上がる。円環状に並ぶ俳優たちの間を、リフレインの台詞が順番に連なることで、言葉が渦を巻くようなループ構造が出現する。特に、クライマックスに配置された「スズメ啼ケ啼ケ、スズメ啼ケ啼ケ、千匹啼ケ万匹啼ケ、千匹啼ケ万匹啼ケ」「セミ啼ケ啼ケ、セミ啼ケ啼ケ、千匹啼ケ万匹啼ケ、千匹啼ケ万匹啼ケ」「カモメ啼ケ啼ケ、カモメ啼ケ啼ケ、千匹啼ケ万匹啼ケ、千匹啼ケ万匹啼ケ」というリフレインは、複数人で同じリズムを刻んで読むことで、身体運動を伴った集団的な祝祭へと高揚していく。海へ向かう行進から、ビートに乗るように体を揺らす集団へ。マラソンランナーや暴走族といった都市の通過者がそこに交差する。「夜明ケマデ、アト何時間？ ドウゾ」「夜明ケマデ、アト三〇分、ドウゾ」、「夜明ケマデ、アト何分？ ドウゾ」「夜明ケマデ、アト三分、ドウゾ」、「夜明ケマデ、アト何分？ ドウゾ」「夜明ケマデ、アト五〇秒、ドウゾ」という通信兵たちが執拗に繰り返すリフレインは、終幕までの時間、「遊び」の時間の終わりを告げるカウントダウンでもある。 ［撮影：井上嘉和］ 一方、本作では、ジェンダーの対称性が（「男たち」「女たち」という集団性と匿名化によっても）極めて明瞭に引かれている構造も浮かび上がる。男たちは、野良犬のように路地を放浪するが、女たちは、「赤いカフェ」「青いカフェ」「桃色のカフェ」と色とりどりのネオンで名指された場所（風俗街）に固定されて動けない。また、「青いカフェの女」は、「あなた、ゲイジュツはもうやめてください」と繰り返し懇願する。「自分を慕って待ち続ける女を振り切ってこそ、男は世俗と隔絶した芸術家になれる」という特権的な芸術家像がここに露呈する。さらには、「女」は芸術家にはなれず、「男＝孤独にさすらう芸術家」をいつまでも待ち続け、優しく抱きしめてくれる存在として描写するジェンダー観も明らかだ。 ビジュアルの要素が強い舞台だからこそ、俳優の声によって戯曲の構造に解像度を上げて迫ることができる。リーディング公演の可能性を提示してくれる機会だった。 鑑賞日：2026/07/05（日） 関連レビュー VISIONEN -ドイツ同時代演劇リーディング・シリーズVol. 9 『HOMOHALAL（ホモハラル）』｜高嶋慈：artscapeレビュー（2019年12月15日号） 松本雄吉 追悼特集｜高嶋慈：artscapeレビュー（2016年12月15日号）

items._cn_summary: 本文评述了为纪念松本雄吉去世10年而推出的朗读剧场《KANIDENKA》，该作基于其1984年初演的《蟹殿下》，以无布景、无视觉装置的朗读形式，将注意力集中在语言的节奏与声呐上。演出通过多位演员的齐声重复、轮唱与循环结构，使台词形成类似音乐的旋律性驱动；剧中大量引入大阪街头招牌、菜单等非戏剧性文字作为朗读文本，将城市日常声音拼贴入作品。从通天阁到南港、再延伸至南海诸岛的空间移动，在声音中构成了航向性的叙事。文章指出，这种朗读形式反而使剧本本质得以显现，语言和声音成为戏剧主体，重构了城市经验，并呈现出集体仪式般的身体性与节奏感。

items.body: August 14 - 16, 2026, Peitz, Germany Up a creaky set of wooden stairs to the lofts of the 1810 Huettenwerk of the historic Ironworks and Fishery Museum of Peitz, an imposing building full of old heavy tools for the iron foundry and fishing works in the surrounding carp ponds, is an exhibition on Free Jazz in the German Democratic Republic (former East Germany). It’s a traveling show, having accompanied Jazzwerkstatt concerts and festivals over the years. The first time I encountered it, at a Globe Unity Orchestra concert in Potsdam in 2014, it prompted me to dig for all of the Amiga Jazz records that I could find, leading to likely the most complete collection of East German jazz in New Jersey. Every year for the past ten years or so that I’ve been to the festival, I find myself drawn to the exhibition, like a pilgrim to worship. Each station of the exhibit offers a glimpse into this well documented but still mythical past, with a final station showcasing the Peitz Festival. Created in 1973 by two young free-thinking music fans, Uli Blobel and Peter “Jimi” Metag, both from the small East German town of Peitz, the festival drew other like minded youth to hear both East German musicians like Ernst-Ludwig Petrowsky and Conny Bauer as well as West German musicians like Alexander von Schlippenbach and other musicians from the other side of the Iron Curtain such as Barry Guy and Wadada Leo Smith. The names are many and the history can be read in the “Woodstock am Karpfenteich’ books as well as experienced here , and the story is a good one. Lasting until shut down by the government in 1982 and restarted by Blobel in 2011 under much different conditions, the Jazzwerkstatt Peitz festival of 2026 still draws some of those who trekked by train and Trabi to the original, but is also working to draw in a new audience whose connection to the past is being built by heading to upper floors via creaky wooden stairs. Starting in 2024, Marie Blobel, the daughter of Uli Blobel, took over. Some of the changes Marie Blobel made included moving the festival from the center of Peitz to the grounds of the fishing museum amidst the carp ponds and injecting a festive flair into the weekend long event. With a packed schedule of concerts and a two kilometer hike to the Doener restaurant, festival goers are oriented to the wurst stand, the home cooked vegetarian dishes at the beer tent and the biergarten around the corner. Kids have the chance to make their own music with an imaginative looping station and everyone can climb aboard the “Karpfenbummler,” an electric miniature train that will take you in style from the festival to town to the train station. Coming into its own it the new form, Jazzwerkstatt Peitz was awarded the Deutsche Jazzpreis this past year. -- Gebhard Ullman’s Hemisphere 4 PLUS (biergarten stage) The concerts began on Friday evening with the folk-meets-modern-jazz sounds of Trio Ivoire . In the trio's music, Hans Lüdemann ’s piano and electronics and Christian Thomé 's percussion and electronics are met with the organic tones of Aly Keïta ’s balafon, an African instrument described as a “ a gourd-resonated xylophone .” The music is upbeat and highly syncopated and thus quickly had some of the at-capacity audience on their feet swaying to their rhythms. As soon as the set ended, the audience began shuffling off, around the museum and cycler hostel (the Gurkenradweg - yes, the Pickle Bikepath - passes by the festival grounds), to a biergarten, where a stage has been set up under a lush copse of trees. Woodwindist Gebhard Ullman ’s newest formation, Hemisphere 4 PLUS , featuring a mix of his current electric and acoustic groups, began with a chamber-jazz like combination of Anna Viechtl ’s harp and Taiko Saito’s vibraphone. Disrupted by a crash of percussion, the group tumbled into a pulsating groove. Describing the music as “sculptures,” Ullmann led the group through an alluring mix of the delicate (add Silke Lange accordion to the chamber jazz components), hard-hitting (with Eric Schaefer on drums and Oliver Potratz on bass) and other-worldly ( Liz Kosack ’s keyboard and synthesizer). OM (main stage) A short shuffle back to the main stage where OM , the legendary avant-jazz-rock group, were ready to go. The original group members, saxophonist Urs Leimgruber , guitarist Christy Doran and bassist Bobby Burri were joined by drummer’s Gerry Hemingway and Tony Buck who have replaced the late Fredy Studer, as they did on the recent Intakt release Suedpol . After a short freely improvised intro from Leimgruber, a blast of rock energy from Doran gave root to a swirling squall of tones and the music slowly evolved into a groove led by the two percussionists. Moments of electric Miles colored the rich panoply of sound which ranged from deeply experimental to outright rock. An excellent set. Closing out the main stage for the evening was the quartet Selvhenter from Copenhagen. Saxophonist Sonja LaBianca and trombonist Maria Bertel and drummers Anja Jacobsen and Jaleh Negari crafted a dark, throbbing techno-jazz designed to get festival goers on their feet. It was quite late by the time the quartet’s final notes faded, but the show wasn’t over … yet, as drummer Willi Kellers and organizer Wolfgang ‘Assi’ Gloede were hosting a jam session in the cozy workshop building behind the main stage. Amongst painted fish sculptures and some serious looking tools, saxophonist Lotte Anker , keyboardist Liz Kosack and bassist Reza Askari joined Kellers in free-jazz improvisation that began with electronic percolations and slowly crescendoing notes that eventually balled into an exciting and thorny tumbleweed of sound. Following the opener, Gloede curated combinations of professional and hobbyist musicians who improvised into the wee hours. -- Wanja Slavin (sitting far right) (church) Saturday’s full schedule began in the town church where saxophonist and festival Improviser-in-Residence Wanja Slavin , last year’s winner of the Brandenburg Jazzpreis - an award developed by Jazzwerkstatt and the state of Brandenburg - debuted a new composition with a band comprised of Peter Evans on trumpet, Leonard Huhn on bass clarinet, Almut Kühne with vocals and Kaja Draksler on piano. The rich 45-minute piece moved seamlessly between moods and approaches as darker moments were balanced by more hopeful passages. Repetitive arpeggios and prominent electronics formed a consistent tonal base accentuated by the dissonant church organ and several outstanding solos. A short while later back at the festival grounds, percussionist and singer Mariá Portugal’s EROSÃO septet took the stage in the rapidly heating up early afternoon. The music began with a brass fanfare as the group walked-on the stage and transitioned to Portugal singing over polyrhythmic accompaniment. Concentrated on a repertoire of songs that drew heavily on her Brazilian background, Portugal’s vocals took center stage, while the high-powered group of saxophonists Lotte Anker and Angelika Niescier , trombonists Matthias Müller and Moritz Wesp , tubist Carl Ludwig Hübsch and bassist Reza Askari provided solid support. Afterwards in the Huettenwerk building, the duo of Mohammad Mostafa Heydarian and Valentin Portron , performing on the traditional Iranian tanbur and bendir - a stringed instrument and hand drum - continued the expansion of the festival’s musical purview. Impro-Concert: Tony Buck, Matthias Mueller, Taito Saito (workshop) Two improvisation sessions, tucked away in the workshop building, injected a bit of the unexpected into the afternoon. The first introduced the British woodwindist Tamar Osborn with the American bassist Nick Dunston and drummer Gerry Hemingway . This first meeting proved fruitful. Clicking quickly, Osborn leaned into the deeper registers of her baritone sax, while Hemingway contributed a lithe, but full, pulse and Dunston provided a melodically swinging bridge between the two. The later improvisation session joined three Berlin based improvisors who have been in each other’s orbits but never played together before. Vibraphonist Taiko Saito , trombonist Matthias Müller and drummer Tony Buck played a set ranging from contemplative to combustive. Aki Takase, Robert Landfermann, Christian Lillinger. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix The mid-afternoon offered both unforgiving sun and an excellent set from pianist Aki Takase who was performing her upbeat, complex, and often humor-laced music with drummer Christian Lillinger and bassist Robert Landfermann on the main stage. The trio’s music is impressive, Lillinger, with his agitated, driving approach is a perfect rhythmic partner for Takase’s own intensity, and Landfermann’s rhythmic and melodic playing adds a nicely fitting layer. Nearing the end of the set, a dramatic moment ensured when Takase suddenly collapsed from the heat. Fortunately, it was reported that the pianist was already on the move to the next concert in Austria that evening. Darius Jones & Otomo Yoshihide Quartet. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix A little later the shows were back in the biergarten, where the trees provided some relief from the 100 degree heat, and the Czech quartet Edemit added a jolt of avant-rock to the day while Neiscer and Portugal picked up in a duo form the earlier set. As the day began to cool, the action moved back on the main stage where Darius Jones and Otomo Yoshihide (alto saxophone and guitar, respectively) augmented by bassist Nick Dunston and drummers Gerald Cleaver and Yasuhiro Yoshigaki provided an electric set. Following a rousing Coltrane-like introduction, the rhythm section gave Jones a rumbling foundation for his soaring melody to which Yoshihide responded with a feedback-laden solo, pushing the music to an early peak. The music ebbed and flowed, from dark atmospheric wanderings to high-energy free-jazz explosions over pulsating rhythms. Afterwards, the UK-based Ill Considered featuring Tamar Osborn ( Idris Rahman on saxophone, Liran Donin on bass, Emre Ramazanoglu on drums and Osborn with various woodwinds) closed out the night with a set heavy on beats and Middle Eastern-tinged scales. The set ended with about half the remaining audience dancing in front of the stage. -- Perhaps in normal times, it would have been a disappointment but after the previous day’s oven-like disposition, the cool, rain-soaked grey morning greeting festival goers on Sunday was welcome. A church service in the Huettenwerk started the day for the faithful while out on the festival yard, the others were huddling under the drink stand tents sipping coffee while the bratwurst man started up his grill. First musical act, Richard Koch’s Ray of Light was the only one to be seen under the steadily raining sky. They began with the trumpeter playing a regal anthem and launching into a cheery, melodic tune filled with the folkish sounds of Fabiana Striffler ’s violin and Valentin Butt ’s accordion along with the rhythm support of Andreas Lang ’s bass and Nora Thiele ’s frame drums. The “gute laune” (good mood) music with its blend of up-tempo jazz, classical and folk elements provided a lighthearted start to another long day of music. Their timing was perfect too, as Ray of Light reached the end of their set, the first beams of sun reached the festival grounds. Have You Ever Been Experienced. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix The opening set was followed by Brandenburg Jazzpreis. Prize winner, guitarist Andreas Willers , who was to present his Hendrix inspired group Have You Ever Been Experienced , featuring a top-notch group of Berlin based musicians: Amy Green on vocals, Rieko Okuda on piano, Jan Roder on bass and Christian Marien on drums, was unfortunately too ill to attend. Despite this, the group, still gave a rousing performance, taking well-worn Hendrix themes and spinning them anew. Okuda took over the guitar solos with a distorted synthesizer, while Roder and Marien made sure the foundations were securely fortified. Most revelatory were Green’s vocals, which retained enough of the melody for song-recognition and enough improvisational liberty to free them from nostalgic interpretation -- for example, an updated interpretation of Allen Ginsberg’s Howl set to a free-jazz take of ‘If 6 was 9.’ The final two sets of the festival moved back into town to the church. The first was the Polish duo of vocalist Maniucha Bikont and bassist Ksawery Wójciński performing a set of haunting folksongs. Discovered through Bikont’s musicology research, the songs came from a disappearing tribe in the Ukraine, with themes that touched on the universal: suffering, responsibility and expecting better manners from the dead. Performed solely with voice and bass, the music filled the church mesmerizingly. Konradism. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix The closing set to the festival may have also been one of the most anticipated. Connecting the festival’s eras, trombonist and archetype of the original Peitz festival and East German free-jazz in general, trombonist Conny Bauer presented the large group Konradisms with an extended composition of “chamber big-band” that mixed generous improvisation and dramatic riffs. Joining Bauer was a cross section of a younger generation of German-based musicians: Nils Wogram on trombone, Maxine Troglauer also on bass trombone, Gerhard Gschlössl on tuba, Claudio Puntin on bass clarinet, Maria Reich on violin, Emily Wittbrodt on cello, Matthias Bauer on bass, Dag Magnus Narvesen on drums and Rieko Okuda on piano. Often breaking into small combos - trombone and piano, tuba and violin - the solos would grow intense and eventually congeal around common themes. A stand out was Puntin whose bass clarinet playing ranged from the sound of a flute to deep, woody resonance. After an intense two and half days of music, the two last concerts were a satisfying and full-circle-moment ending to the festival. Overall, one could sense a tilt towards the new - nights that ended with experimental but danceable music, a series of risky but successful workshop concerts with musicians meeting for the first time, an infusion of world-music elements, and a loosening, but not denying, deference to the past, showing a way forward. More about the Peitz festival: Review of the 50th Anniversary Peitz Festival Review of the Jazzwerkstatt Peitz Boxset Jazzwerkstatt Peitz website . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 本文报道了德国 Jazzwerkstatt Peitz 音乐节的历史与现场。该音乐节起源于东德时期，由两位自由思想青年创办，曾聚集东西德及国际即兴乐手，后遭政府取缔，2011年重启，现由创办人之女接棒，迁至鲤鱼池塘旁的渔业博物馆园区，融入市集、儿童音乐装置和小火车等节庆元素，并荣获德国爵士乐奖。演出方面，周五以 Trio Ivoire 开场，作品融合民谣与现代爵士，钢琴与电子声响交织。文章将音乐节置于东德自由爵士的谱系中，既追溯其传奇过往，也呈现年轻一代带来的革新，展现自由即兴在当代语境下的延续与在地化实践。

items.excerpt: アルカディア弦楽四重奏団によるヴァインベルクの弦楽四重奏曲全集が遂に完結した。2020年に第1巻がリリースされてから6年、全6枚の最後を飾る第6巻が完結盤となる。旧ソ連の作曲家ミェチスワフ・ヴァインベルクは同国を代表する作曲家ショスタコーヴィチの後輩世代にあたり、生涯に17の弦楽四重奏曲を書いた。また両者は互いに作風へ影響を及ぼし合った事でも知られている。これまで彼の弦楽四重奏曲全集は、2014年にダネル四重奏団（CPO）、2023年にシレジア四重奏団（Accord）によって録音されており、アルカディア弦楽四重奏団による本全集は、それに続く3例目となる。

items._cn_summary: 阿尔卡迪亚弦乐四重奏团完成了米奇斯瓦夫·魏因贝格弦乐四重奏全集的第六卷，收录第10、12、17号等作品。魏因贝格是苏联作曲家，与肖斯塔科维奇相互影响，该系列自2020年起陆续发行，本卷为整套录音的收官之作。全集以弦乐四重奏形式呈现作曲家不同时期的创作面貌，尤其展现了他在传统体裁中独特的和声语汇与戏剧性表达。阿尔卡迪亚四重奏的演奏注重声部平衡与结构把握，在乐句处理上兼具抒情性和紧张感，完整呈现了魏因贝格对弦乐四重奏体裁的持续探索。此前已有丹尼尔与西里西亚两个四重奏团的全集录音，本版是第三个完整版本，乐评着重指出其作为系列完结篇的意义，对于关注现代弦乐文献的听众而言，这套录音提供了系统的聆听路径。

items.body: The year of blue continues: blue art, blue music, blue moods. Klara Lewis‘ Opening is an azure version of the hue, twisting and turning like permutations seen beneath varying degrees of light. The first single and opening track “Ta Min Hand” establishes the baseline from which the album will drift, like a small vessel upon the sea. Even the music includes waves. A sweet melody emerges, loops and abrades. In “City,” solo piano plays over the sounds of traffic and conversation, momentarily pausing as if to listen to the other acoustic sources. Suddenly a more aggressive set of sounds conquers the sonic field, a helicopter of rovers and gears. The piano reenters, insistent, then the conversation, posing questions about where the attention turns in an economy of sonic competition. The more orchestral “Vaknar” (“Waking”) attempts to soothe, but the ground has already proven unstable. The looping continues, but the volume increases. Opening revels in juxtaposition and incremental shift. “Feel” and “Drip” were composed for Mika Taanila’s expressive film “Failed Emptiness,” which toys with expectations of light. As the album’s most abrasive piece, “Feel” stands in contrast to the melodies that haunt the earlier selections. The brief “Drip” is its polar opposite, nearly a dance piece, restricted only by its length, the connecting tissue a feedback drone emerging toward the end. “Tide,” by far the album’s longest piece at 11:37, is dedicated to Christine Ödlund’s painting “Dissolving Strawberry,” and is also on a compilation EP that finds connections between pigment and tone. While listening, one gleans melodies through gauze, origins obscured like fragments of forgotten lyrics. By “How Far?” abstraction begins to win over form, Lewis’ voice suddenly emerging in the center as another instrument. Furthering the sense of inversion, the set closer is called “Opening,” making one wonder if the title may mean an opening, such as a pathway or door; or the sense of opening one’s self to unpredictability or the divine. By the time the album ends, one has been led down multiple pathways, and even the trail of string has become tangled. To find one’s bearings, one must return to the beginning or plunge further into the unknown. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: experimental electronic / ambient / drone / abstract / contemporary composition
items._cn_summary: Klara Lewis 的《Opening》以蓝色为意象贯穿全作，旋律如小船在声浪中漂移。专辑通过拼贴与并置手法构建层次：钢琴在交通与对话声中进退，侵略性噪音偶尔打断平衡；部分曲目为影像作品所作，呈现出从抒情旋律到高强度摩擦音的极端对比。十一分半的《Tide》以薄纱般的碎片化旋律探讨声音与颜料的对应关系；末曲《Opening》让人声作为乐器浮现，模糊了形式与抽象的边界。整张专辑在旋律循环、渐进式音量和声场竞争之间游走，将听众引入多条相互缠绕的路径，最终指向一个既可视为入口也可视为深渊的开放状态。
