items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — One might associate Chile with the folk songs of V�ctor Jara, the psychedelic and progressive past of Los Jaivas, or high-quality pop-rock bands like La Ley; yet Cherc�n offers a pleasant surprise with a bold, distinctive rock sound that draws from psychedelia while incorporating a jazz-infused saxophone and string arrangements, featuring violin and cello, that add nuance to the quintet's (and its guests') fast-paced progressive rock style."La culpa" is the opening track, reminiscent of The Mars Volta in its wild, defiant nature, where the sound builds toward a final climax, intensifying as if funneling through the guitar; the audio distorts while Mart�n Pe�a, the vocalist, belts out vocals that are at once melodic and visceral. There are moments of great freedom, reminiscent of jazz scat singing, that shift into free-jazz passages blended with hard rock. This fusion, combined with the vocalist's delivery (which at times resembles a mystical, inverted prayer), reaches a new level of decibel intensity and opens up a new dimension for the saxophone within progressive heavy rock, distinct from the styles of Van der Graaf Generator (a feat that once seemed impossible) or Gong, two major touchstones for the instrument in this genre. Here, the fusion is more contemporary, yet Kalimba still retains melody and harmony, in abundance, while incorporating folk influences drawn from indigenous music.The instrumental sections still sound as improvised and fresh as when they must have been composed; when the band kicks into highly intricate, distorted rock, backed by the string section, the music gains added weight without losing any power; quite the opposite. Mart�n Pe�a holds his own as a vocalist, knowing exactly how to function as yet another instrument.Tiempos paralelos can serve as a summary of Cherc�n's musical approach, as the first part involves the saxophone and a sense of restraint, while the second features an uprising led by the guitar and a defiant vocal performance, delivering a solo reminiscent of Annie Haslam channeling Ian Gillan. "Las Mentiras del Muro" opens with a powerful foundation of drums and bass that reminded me of the overflowing energy of Rage Against the Machine, though the comparison stops at the vocals, as Mart�n Pe�a handles both the metal and progressive sections with the same care and precision found in the saxophone notes; the sax, for all its delicacy, sounds no less powerful and truly stands out as a key protagonist of the album."Relato de una obsesi�n", specifically its first part, titled "Quimera", features Eastern percussion and rhythms; the quintet achieves such a profound communion that they seem to act as one, wholly absorbed in the task of capturing their vision for posterity. The second part, "El orate," erupts, unleashing the inevitable, a tidal surge that can no longer be contained. It embodies that Eastern-inspired tensi�n, held taut to the point of infinity, until it finally meets the resistance it had ultimately sought, and that fiery blaze, which was in fact its very reason for being, is consumed.As if the ashes still held light and heat after the fire, the album's final track, "Colores," embodies a mysticism that retains its clarity, refusing to be blinded by its own nature, and one that learns and evolves, promising a future that will harvest the seeds sown in this auspicious debut.

items._cn_summary: 这是一支来自智利的五人乐团，将迷幻摇滚的狂野与传统进步摇滚的复杂结构作为骨架，融入爵士萨克斯与弦乐（小提琴、大提琴）的编制。主唱 Martín Peña 的演唱兼具旋律性与爆发力，在硬摇滚段落中呈现出近似自由爵士的即兴自由度。专辑中多处引入东欧打击乐节奏与原住民音乐元素，形成跨文化融合的质感。器乐段落保留了即兴的新鲜感，弦乐组的加入为失真吉他音墙增添了层次与重量而非削弱力量。萨克斯在此被赋予了独立的主角地位，突破了范德格拉夫发生器或 Gong 等乐队中该乐器的传统用法。整张专辑在结构上具有明显的渐进性，从内敛的开场逐步推向高潮，制造出强烈的张力与释放感。

items.body: And so, as summer draws to a close and we enter the ever-popular fall season (which affords us the use of the word “autumnal”, which you fucking bet we’ll be working in wherever possible), we also enter the final third of 2026. Of course, needing to get our Year End coverage done and dusted by mid-December means we’ve got roughly three months left of coverage, and the actual determination of what records we liked the most still to come. As always, suggestions of things we’ve overlooked are always welcome, as are your own picks, feel free to toss ’em in the comments below. But of course, this is all a preamble for our most venerable tradition, ye olde Tracks post. Join us won’t you? Creux Lies Pig, “An American Ideal of Beauty” Raymond Watts sure is a busy guy these days. Aside from a massive tour he’s kicking off across North America, the Pig mastermind is following up this year’s enjoyable Hurt People Hurt with a smattering of follow-up EPs. The first of those, from which the track embedded below is taken, is Dirt Box, featuring four new tracks with accompanying remixes by the likes of Stabbing Westward, Combichrist, Cyanotic and Rabbit Junk. Then we’ve got Merciless coming down the pike, a remix EP with cuts by Clock DVA (!!) and Pitchshifter amongst others. I guess you can’t keep a good hog down. Dirt Box by PIG Creux Lies, “Jubilate” Man, but Sacramento’s Creux Lies are keeping us on our toes. The depth and richness of sophomore LP Goodbye Divine has us waiting on a follow-up with bated breath, but the third original track they’ve released over the past couple of years sounds very distinct from its predecessors. Here, they’re in an easily approachable synth dancefloor mode, but the real sauce is in the slowburn approach Ean Elliot Clevenger takes to the vocals which build across its runtime. Jubilate by Creux Lies UNTER STRØM, “Stumbling” UNTER STRØM is the side-project of Alex from LA’s post-punkers Matte Blvck, and while it is a more down the pipe electronic project than its parent band, it’s a far cry from the defacto sound of modern electro-darkwave. Indeed, while the sound of their material is certainly of a more shadowy cast, you’re getting programming and arrangements that refer to more aboveground sounds in the world of progressive house and melodic techno, splitting the difference between those bright club nights and dark underground dancefloors in fine fashion. Between Forms by UNTER STRØM alarm!systemen, “Burn” Don’t let the apparent compositional simplicity of Belgian newcomers alarm!systemen’s approach to melancholy coldwave on this track fool you; there’s a real consideration of colour and harmony here which makes a virtue of modern gear and technique rather than eschewing it for the sage of nostalgia, while shooting a style familiar to fans of any number of early 80s continental acts with a bright and fresh strain of dreampop. alarm!systemen by alarm!systemen Evil Dust, “Sadistic” Some good n’ gnarly lo-fi business from London body music act Evil Dust, whose new LP I Just Want to Fit In is due shortly on the 11th of September. If’n you like some of the stuff that the whole industrialized techno sound was doing, but wish it was, well, more industrial, this might fit the bill; heavily percussive, lots of sample work, and an unruly groove that never quite settles in where you think it will. I JUST WANT TO FIT IN by EVIL DUST Einhänder Aus Stahl, “4 Meter Punch To The Face (Visitor remix)” Speaking of lo-fi body music, the new maxi EP from Einhänder Aus Stahl, the side project of Micheal of Chrome Corps, offers a slew of minimal tracks which strip throwback techno and EBM to their barest skeleton. Throw in a little bit of left-field synth-funk courtesy of Visitor (you probably don’t need us to ID the samples for you) and you have a twitchy, burpy blast of fun. Mebyon Kernow by Einhänder Aus Stahl The post Tracks: August 31st, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.album: Tomorrows Letters Puts the Mind on Trial with Noir Synthpop Single “Up Against the Wall”
items.excerpt: The whispers in my mind, the echoes of my past, Judgment in the mirror, a reflection that will last. The mind can build a courtroom from almost nothing. items.body: The whispers in my mind, the echoes of my past, Judgment in the mirror, a reflection that will last. The mind can build a courtroom from almost nothing. A remembered phrase becomes evidence, an old mistake is summoned as a witness, and conscience takes the prosecutor’s table before crossing the room to pronounce sentence from the bench. No counsel appears for the defense, no statute of limitations applies, and every hour spent alone provides another opportunity to reopen the case. On Up Against the Wall, Minsk-based artist Tomorrows Letters turns this internal proceeding into a severe and stylish piece of noir synthpop. The solo project of Kiryl Karotki, Tomorrows Letters enters the song already cornered, facing a tribunal in which the accused, prosecutor, and judge occupy the same body. A low, saxophone-like drone opens the recording before giving way to a mechanized groove. Sparse piano notes land beside Karotki’s controlled vocal, lending each phrase the gravity of sworn testimony. His delivery remains cold and composed, yet there is considerable force beneath that restraint, like silk draped across the song’s dread. Trip-hop menace and industrial textures run through the rhythm, meeting the darker electronic pop associated with Depeche Mode’s 1990s and early-2000s records. The clipped construction also carries the severe elegance of 1980s new wave and minimal synth. When the saxophone returns between verses, it winds through organ-like keys and a low electronic buzz, giving the track the character of a neo-noir jazz performance conducted inside a machine. Karotki’s voice completes the setting, transporting the listener into a room filled with stark light, suspended haze, and hard silhouettes. Every word appears carefully measured, as though an answer given too quickly could become further evidence for the prosecution. The lyrics make this psychological trial explicit. Past mistakes supply the testimony, the mirror preserves the verdict, and the heartbeat keeps time for fear. Within the “courtroom of my soul,” the singer bears every role and pays every toll. By the outro, the narrow line between right and wrong has become another instrument of captivity: “I’m a prisoner of my own mind.” “The song describes a state where your own mind acts as both the prosecutor and the judge in a trial that never ends,” Karotki explains. “It’s about being your own worst enemy, trapped in a loop of self-judgment where conscience acts as a punisher rather than a moral guide.” The single release of Up Against the Wall, the first offering from Karotki’s debut LP set for release this autumn. It is accompanied by an exclusive remix from Karotki’s friends in Nürnberg, marking the first of several guest appearances and collaborations planned for the forthcoming album. The song was mixed and mastered by Nürnberg’s sound engineer, Andrei Bobrovka, while its cover artwork was created by Tomorrows Letters. Tomorrows Letters is a project that operates according to a strict hardware-only philosophy, with Karotki using vintage samplers and unconventional songwriting methods to give it a dusty, tactile character. New Romantic and minimal synth-pop influences provide the foundation, though their historical language is put in the service of present-day psychological estrangement. Across his work, Karotki examines isolation, self-judgment, Jungian ideas concerning the hidden self, maladaptive daydreaming, compulsive creation, and the pursuit of victories that prove empty once attained. Listen to Up Against the Wall below: Follow Tomorrows Letters: Instagram Bandcamp Spotify YouTube Apple Music The post “Judgment in the Mirror” — Tomorrows Letters Puts the Mind on Trial with Noir Synthpop Single “Up Against the Wall” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Sixteen years in, Mondträume have a different singer, a double album and, for the first time, confirmed live dates. “Mind Games” came out on Alfa Matrix on 26 June 2026 as a 24-track 2CD, the Spanish synthpop project’s third album and its first full-length with Nicky Schulschenk on vocals. In this interview Pikotto talks about how the collaborations on the record doubled as an audition process, why a previously unreleased Bruderschaft remix ended up on it, and what the current line-up actually is. On that last point he corrects the record: Mondträume is a duo of himself and Schulschenk, with Madil Hardis and Ivan Derbenev friends and collaborators rather than members. Mind Games (Deluxe Edition) by MONDTRÄUME Mondträume interview SL: Mondträume turns 16 this year, and the lineup has changed almost completely since 2010 – Damasius Venys left for Mental Exile in 2020, Ivan Derbenev and Madil Hardis joined in 2022, and Nicky Schulschenk has fronted the band since “Heart Machine” in 2023. What’s the one thing about writing a Mondträume song that has never changed through all of that, and what’s changed the most? Pikotto: First of all, I’d like to thank you for inviting me to take part in this interview. It’s quite amazing to think that 16 years have already passed!!!!!! Where has all that time gone? Looking back, I think the one thing that has never changed is the passion and excitement I still feel when I create music. The melodies continue to move between melancholy and happiness, and I still have the same desire to make music that can touch people, make them feel something, and ultimately allow them to enjoy the journey through each song. That is something I don’t think will ever change. In that sense, I don’t really feel that I have changed as an artist. I think the journey has simply taken a different direction. The road may have turned, but the essence remains the same: the way I approach composition, the emotions behind the melodies, and above all, the desire to keep creating. The biggest difference is that today, those songs have a new voice. Nicky has brought a new dimension and a new identity to the music, but the heart of what I want to express through my compositions is still very much the same. So perhaps the direction has changed, but the feeling that started this journey 16 years ago is still there. And as long as I continue to feel that excitement when I hear a melody come to life, I don’t see that changing anytime soon. SL: “Lovers, Sinners & Liars” took five years to finish because of health issues you were dealing with at the time. Did that experience change how you pace yourself as a songwriter, and did any of it shape how “Mind Games” came together? Pikotto: Not at all. In fact, if anything had changed, I would say it has changed for the better. It feels almost like being given a second chance – a chance to climb out of a dark place and start believing again that things can get better. When someone is struggling with their health or going through difficult circumstances in life, you can reach a point where you simply don’t feel like doing anything. Everything can suddenly seem as if it has come to an end. I think that is one of the biggest mistakes we make as human beings. Deep down, we know we should keep fighting and moving forward, but sometimes there is something inside us that blocks us and makes it incredibly difficult to take that next step. And unfortunately, no matter how much we want to fight it, it can be very hard to overcome. With “Mind Games”, I knew from the very beginning that it was going to be a difficult journey. We had a new singer, a new musical direction, and a lot of things that were unfamiliar to us. That made me want to give everything I had to this album. And looking at everything that has happened since its release – the reviews, the comments from listeners, and even the Spotify statistics, where we went from around 3,000 monthly listeners to more than 15,000 – I honestly feel that we have achieved something really special. We also spent several weeks at number two on the GEWC Top 15 as one of the best albums on the chart, which was an incredible feeling. When you put all of that together and see the response that “Mind Games” has been receiving, I can honestly say that I’m extremely proud of what we have accomplished. I truly believe we have done a great job, and I’m very satisfied with the result. And above all, I have to thank Nicky from the bottom of my heart for coming on board this journey, getting on this ship with me, and helping me make all of this possible. I honestly couldn’t be happier to have him alongside me for this new chapter of Mondträume. SL: “Mind Games” runs to 24 tracks across two CDs. Why a double album rather than a shorter, tighter release, and how did you decide what made the final cut versus what got held back? Pikotto: Well, this was something Seba from Alfa Matrix (I like to take this opportunity to send him a big hello from here) and I discussed At first, I had the idea of releasing the albums separately: the third Mondträume album with the new official vocalist, and a second album that would be more like a “Pikotto & Friends” project… or something along those lines. Just one of those crazy ideas that occasionally goes through my head, haha! But in the end, Seba and I decided to put everything together as a double CD, and honestly, I’m really happy with how it turned out. I think it was the right decision. In fact, I designed the entire visual side of the booklet myself 🙂 So it was a very personal project for me, not only musically but visually as well. As for what was left out, there are a couple of songs that never quite came together in my mind the way I wanted them to. And then there’s another one that, to be completely honest, I simply forgot to include! With so many things going through my head, I was bound to forget something at some point. I’m a disaster. And it’s actually a great remix by the […] Gerrit Thomas of the song “I Need You Now”. So I promise that it won’t be forgotten forever – I’m planning to release it on a future EP dedicated to that song. I guess sometimes even the songs that don’t make it onto the album end up having a second life of their own. SL: The album brings in guest vocalists from District 13, Neon Space Men, Color Theory, and Antilav. How did each of those collaborations happen, and did you write with a specific voice in mind before reaching out, or after? Pikotto: Well, I actually used these collaborations as a way of searching for a new singer. During that period, I was trying to figure out what direction to take and how I could find the right voice for Mondträume. One day, while talking to a great fan of ours, Alain (who is also a wonderful person) he suggested that I should try looking for a new vocalist through collaborations like these. In fact, he was the one who put me in contact with the singers involved. “Pictures of You” was born during that particular period of my life, while I was creating these songs and experimenting with different voices. But the moment I heard Nicky’s voice, the vocal melody, and the way his voice blended with the musical foundation I had created, I immediately fell in love with the combination. At that moment, I already knew exactly who I wanted to become the new official voice of Mondträume. I made the proposal to him, and, well… you all know how the story ended. 🙂 So, to answer the second part of the question, yes – all of the musical foundations were created before I contacted the singers. The collaborations came afterwards, as part of the process of finding the voice that would ultimately lead Mondträume into this new chapter. SL: The record also includes a previously unreleased Mondträume remix made for Bruderschaft. What’s the story behind that remix, and why put it on this album instead of releasing it on its own? Pikotto: This is quite a delicate subject for me, and the first thing I would like to do is send a huge hug to the great Rexx, wherever he may be. I hope that he has finally found peace and is happy. As many of you will know, he sadly passed away after battling that terrible disease, cancer. It was a devastating loss for the music scene, and my deepest thoughts and strength go to his family and loved ones. I actually made this remix quite a long time ago, when Rexx contacted me and asked if I would like to take part in the project. I didn’t hesitate for a second. Rexx and I were basically the only two people who had heard that remix for a very long time. He had nothing but praise for it, and his words really encouraged me and gave me a lot of motivation. Unfortunately, though, He never seemed to find the right moment to release it. When I finished the third album, I contacted Rexx and asked for his permission to include the remix on the album. He kindly gave me his blessing, and for me, that was a huge honour. Including it on the album means much more to me than simply adding another remix. It is my way of keeping his memory alive and making sure that, in some small way, Rexx will always have a place within our music and within the history of Mondträume. I will always be grateful to him for that. SL: Nicky joined as vocalist on “Heart Machine” in December 2023. Two years and a full album later, is he still primarily a vocalist, or is he shaping arrangements and lyrics now too? Pikotto: Nicky is mainly responsible for the vocals, and the lyrics come entirely from his own creativity and imagination. As I mentioned before, I’m extremely happy with him. I think he has an incredible voice, and it fits the synthpop style of Mondträume perfectly. That said, there have been a few occasions when he has said to me, “Hey, what if you did the melody like this at this particular point?” And sometimes those little suggestions can actually lead us somewhere really interesting. The truth is that working with him is both very easy and a lot of fun. We understand each other really well, and the creative process feels very natural between us. In a relatively short time, I think we’ve also developed a really strong friendship, which makes everything even more enjoyable. At the end of the day, when you can work with someone, create music together, have a laugh along the way, and genuinely enjoy the process, I think you’ve found something pretty special. SL: Madil Hardis, who joined Mondträume in 2022, put out a solo charity EP called “Noel” that same year. How involved is he in Mondträume day to day now, and does the rest of the current lineup – him and Ivan Derbenev – have room for outside projects like that? Pikotto: I have a very strong friendship with both of them. They are not official members of Mondträume. Mondträume is a duo consisting of Pikotto and Nicky. It’s true that we did try to work together as a group for a while, but I eventually realised that it wasn’t really the direction I wanted to take Mondträume in. That doesn’t change the fact that I have a great friendship with both of them, and I’m very grateful for everything we have created together. Madil has an absolutely spectacular voice, and I’m sure we will continue working together on future collaborations and features. SL: Side-Line called Mondträume one of the strongholds of “the 3rd electropop wave” a few years back, and ranked your debut among the best synthpop albums of the last four decades. Sixteen years in, does that kind of legacy talk change how you approach a new record, or do you try to ignore it? Pikotto: For me, that was a huge honour. Being mentioned among some of the great albums with my very first album… just imagine! It was something truly incredible and something I will always be grateful for. But honestly, it doesn’t influence me when I’m creating new music. Of course, whenever I’m asked about Mondträume, I’m very happy to mention those achievements, but they are not something I think about when I sit down to compose a new album. What I always try to do is make every new song something special for the people who listen to us and, above all, make them feel something. That is actually my biggest concern – not whether an album will be considered one of the best, but whether I will manage to create something that connects emotionally with the listener. That is what really matters to me. And, so far, I think I’m achieving it. If, in the future, another Mondträume album is once again considered one of the best albums, I will obviously be incredibly grateful and very happy about it, and I certainly hope it happens. But, as I said, it’s not something I’m constantly looking out for or worrying about. I simply want to keep making music that makes people feel something. Everything else is a wonderful bonus. SL: You’ve kept an unmistakable 80s touch since day one. With 24 new tracks on “Mind Games,” was there ever a temptation to push further away from that reference point, or does the project only really work within it? Pikotto: I really love the music of the 80s, and I think that definitely comes through in my compositions. But it’s not really a question of whether I want to move away from that sound or not. When I sit down to compose, I simply let my hands and my mind do what they naturally want to do. The melodies that come to me often have that unmistakable 80s feeling, and I feel very comfortable working that way. It’s simply part of who I am as a composer and the musical language I’ve developed over the years. Maybe at some point the musical direction will change a little, who knows? But somehow, whenever I try to move too far away from it, my mind seems to travel straight back to the 80s because that’s where it feels most at home. Hahaha! I guess you can take the composer out of the 80s, but you can’t take the 80s out of the composer! SL: “Poisoned Love” was included on Side-Line’s “United 2 – The Odin Files” compilation for Ukraine this July. What made you say yes to that specific compilation, and would Mondträume take part in benefit releases like it again? Pikotto: I believe that compilations like these, created to support a meaningful cause (whether it’s helping those affected by war, fighting diseases, or raising awareness for important issues) are always worth supporting. Being able to contribute, even in a small way, is something I feel is very important. We all have the opportunity to make a difference, no matter how big or small our contribution may be, and I think we should all do our part whenever we can. Music has always had the power to bring people together, inspire solidarity, and support those who need it most. If a song, an album, or a compilation can help achieve that, then I’m more than happy to be involved. And that also answers your second question: yes, absolutely. I will continue to participate in these kinds of projects whenever I have the opportunity. Supporting a good cause through music is something I will always be proud to do. SL: What’s next for Mondträume after “Mind Games” – live shows, a new lineup configuration, or time off before the next release? Pikotto: I hope the future has great things in store for us. As I mentioned earlier, the official Mondträume line-up is the one featured on this album: Nicky will be the voice at the front, while I will continue to focus on the music and production side. One of our main goals for 2027 is to start bringing Mondträume to the stage. In fact, we already have two shows confirmed: February 27th in Leeds (UK) and March 6th in Madrid. We are also very close to finalising another show in Mexico, and hopefully many more opportunities will follow. I’m also pleased to announce that we have recently signed a non-exclusive agreement with Dark Entries Spain, and our management will be handled by Barbara Banu. If anyone is interested in booking Mondträume, they are welcome to contact Barbara through her social media channels, or they can reach out to me directly. It would be a genuine pleasure for us to bring our live show to as many places as possible and connect with audiences around the world. And as for free time… I think I’ve already had more than enough of that! Now it’s time to get moving, work hard, and give it everything we’ve got. We have a lot of exciting plans ahead, and I can’t wait to see where this new chapter takes us. Hahaha! As always, it is a genuine pleasure have this kind of one-to-one conversation with Side-Line. Thank you for your interest in Mondträume, for your support over the years, and for helping us share our music with your readers. We truly appreciate it. About Mondträume Mondträume is a synthpop project formed in 2010 and based in Spain, built around producer and composer Pikotto. Damasius Venys sang on the early records before leaving in 2020 for Mental Exile. Ivan Derbenev and Madil Hardis worked with the project from 2022, and Nicky Schulschenk took over vocals with the “Heart Machine” EP in December 2023. The line-up is now a duo of Pikotto and Schulschenk. The project has released through Alfa Matrix since its debut, which Side-Line placed among the strongest synthpop albums of the past four decades, and followed with “Lovers, Sinners & Liars”, a record that took five years to complete. The single “Poisoned Love” arrived in December 2024 and was expanded into a digital EP in February 2025, alongside a previous Side-Line interview. The track was later included on Side-Line’s Ukraine charity compilation “United 2 – The Odin Files” in July 2026. Alfa Matrix announced “Mind Games” in April 2026 and released it on 26 June. The 24 tracks split between new songs and remixes, with guest vocals from Madil Hardis on “Immortal”, “Day After Day” and “Whole”, District 13 on “I Tried So Hard” and “Please Don’t Cry”, Neon Space Men on “Heart”, Color Theory on “Better Off” and Antilav on “Falling Snow” and “Something”. The remix side carries reworkings by Code 64, Final Selection, Rob Dust, Beyond Border and Neon Space Men, plus the Mondträume remix of Bruderschaft’s “Falling”. The Leeds and Madrid dates in early 2027 will be the project’s first live shows.

items.body: Band:  Jordsjø | Album: Pestkrønikene | Genre: Progressive rock, Heavy psych | Year: 2026 From: Oslo, Norway | Label: Dying Victims Productions For fans of: Anekdoten, Wobbler, Uriah Heep, Rush Bandcamp This is far from the first time Jordsjø has been featured on this site. They’re among the most prominent names in the flourishing Norwegian prog scene, and their music is usually pretty solid. Their last release, the split LP Kontraster with Breidablik, featured some of their best work ever. What I love about  Jordsjø’s usual work is the way they integrate classic Anglo-prog elements with ample Nordic folk flavors. Pestkrønikene (Eng.: The Plague Chronicles), then, marks something of a break from their usual style. The music here is much heavier, harder, and fuzzier, drawing from classic heavy psych sounds. It’s certainly different from their usual output, but it’s another strong entry in their discography. Pestkrønikene opens with its title track. Dramatic stabs of organ and Mellotron eventually lead into a hazy, murky milieu. Flute helps lend some levity; the sharpness cuts through the thickness of everything else quite nicely. Jordsjø doesn’t completely ditch their folk roots here, with a brief interlude in the second half providing some good contrast. “White Magic” features guest vocals from Jon Henriksen of Norwegian heavy metal band Black Magic. Flavors of 1960s psychedelia are prominent with the dreamy vocals and acoustic backing. Even when crunchier tones come in, they harken back to the late ’60s and early ’70s, as opposed to more modern metal. “Seven Heads” is based around an askew blues riff, and this is simply not one of the best songs on the album. Jordsjø is a talented band that can play a lot of different music quite well, but blues is a genre that feels somewhat clunky coming from them. They (more briefly) dabbled in the blues on the two preceding songs, and those moments were similarly weak in comparison. At least the second half of this song features some fun and exciting instrumental moments. The instrumental “Kaosvelde – Vasallens Elegi” (“Chaos Fields – Vasallen’s Elegy”) is more in Jordsjø’s typical wheelhouse. Flute and acoustic guitar are supported by synth and Mellotron, and this functions as a nice interlude. That is followed by another instrumental, “Kaosveldets Endelikt” (“End of the Chaos Fields”), featuring Lars Fredrik Frøislie of Wobbler on organ. This is the heaviest cut on the album, and it’s also the most convincing Jordsjø has been as a metal band (by 1970s standards).  We get another Wobbler guest feature on “The Awakened”, with Andreas Prestmo providing vocals. This song sees Jordsjø bust out their best Rush impression. The guitar chords are distinctly Lifesonian, and the riffs are complex and muscular. Prestmo’s vocals, as usual, are more evocative of Jon Anderson than Geddy Lee, and this combination helps to keep this cut from being simple Rush-aping. “Spiritual Lament” features drummer Kristian Valbo in a guest appearance, and he makes the most of his time here. Where “The Awakened” felt like a Rush song for its guitar parts, this feels like one for its drumming. Valbo clearly takes a lot of inspiration from Neil Peart, especially in his complex, tom-heavy fills. (There are some quite Rush-y guitar and synth parts on this cut, too.) Jon Henriksen makes one final appearance on this album’s last song, “Talisman II”. This feels the most like a typical Jordsjø song of any piece on this album. There are plenty of obvious tributes to early ’70s hard rock, but the band’s usual prog-folk stylings are prominent throughout. Jordsjø’s foray into hard rock is an interesting experiment. It’s not the band’s best album, but I like it. It’s fun to hear a band paying homage to their influences while also bringing their usual character along.  Score: 74/100

items._cn_summary: Jordsjø 的《Pestkrønikene》偏离了乐队以往北欧民谣与前卫摇滚的融合路线，转向更沉重、更模糊的重型迷幻声响。标题曲用戏剧化的管风琴和 Mellotron 营造阴郁氛围，长笛穿透厚重音墙带来轻盈对比。'White Magic' 邀来 Black Magic 主唱 Jon Henriksen，呈现60年代晚期迷幻色彩；器乐曲'Kaosvelde – Vasallens Elegi'回归长笛与原声吉他的典型搭配，而'Kaosveldets Endelikt'在 Wobbler 成员 Lars Fredrik Frøislie 的管风琴加持下成为专辑最沉重的段落。'The Awakened' 由 Andreas Prestmo 演唱，展示了复杂的 Rush 式强力和弦。乐评指出蓝调段落相对笨拙，但整体仍是乐队又一张扎实的作品。

items.body: Patience is said to be a virtue, but in a time of waiting, it can feel like anything but. The Sweet Wait is a collaboration between Spanish ambient / experimental composer Pepo Galán and Australian dreampop vocalist Karen Vogt. When united together, their music becomes elegant and emotional. As indicated by its title, The Sweet Wait explores themes of patience, the relinquishing of the ego, and ultimate surrender, which, in a world where control is everything, is sought after, is valued above all else, can be a difficult concept to grasp. Taking in dark ambient, dreampop, shoegaze, neo-classical, and ambient elements, their debut record is a sweet blending, with affection and love leaking out from its sound, tracing river-lines through its haunting ambient geography, which contains a guitar echoing with want, an elderly piano, a younger set of swirling vocals, still yearning to receive and trailing behind in the ambient slipstream, and a creaking cello. It’s about absence and doubt, because during a season of waiting, things can feel like a dead end, like all hope has been lost. But it’s also an album of acceptance in surrender (which is not the same as resignation), and of deep humility to even consider surrendering. Written and recorded between Paris and Malaga, the music is a beautiful blurring between Pepo’s elegant, sweeping, and deeply textured ambient soundscapes and Karen’s vocals, which glitter from in-between, unobtrusively carving out a space in the ambient sound, which at times is oceanic, and adding to it further with degrees of delicacy and humility. Karen co-founded the dreampop group Heligoland, and her vocals have always been a vital part of the group’s output; the same is true here. A dream-like, lyrical ambient is made real, the words air-swimming In a society that places instant gratification on a pedestal, waiting can be viewed as a difficult thing. As Queen once demanded, ‘I want it all, and I want it now’. But there is a sweetness and an innocence in waiting, a patient mind cultivating calmness and confidence, as well as a deep knowledge that things will eventually come to light, given time. It doesn’t have to be all doom and gloom; it doesn’t have to be hard. While one cannot control outside influences and events, one can control the response. The Sweet Wait features two stunning photographs from French photographer Aurélie Scouarnec, who captures darkness, shadows, and life between the veils. The sacred, the reverent, and the extremely precious nature of life and the delicacy of a single moment, where the hidden is as important as the revealed, unfolds within each photograph. So too are things concealed when waiting, and with patience. A strong will is required. Everything has its season; the fruit will ripen. The Sweet Wait by GALÁN / VOGT www.galanvogt.bandcamp.com

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. More to hear: United States of Alchemy - Songs of Compassion (Review) Dani Jan� - Vida (Review)

items._cn_summary: Alison Cotton 的《The Gods Laugh》延续了她标志性的模糊边界风格，将民谣、前卫实验与宗教性感知融为一体。中提琴、簧风琴、击弦古钢琴与钢琴构成核心编制，同时引入鼓、贝斯与合成器拓展音色维度。多数曲目为即兴演奏、单次录制，弥漫着神秘而静谧的氛围，旋律仿佛穿越时空撷取自古老民歌。专辑核心曲目《Sprigs of Heather》以中世纪圣咏为引，发展为钢琴主导的缓慢级进旋律；《I Am!》为约翰·克莱尔诗作谱曲，在持续低音之上呈现超脱的吟唱。这是一张献给2024年末去世的父亲的纪念之作，失落感贯穿始终，尤其在《The Final Harvest》中以庄严笔触缅怀父亲最后一次造访他所钟爱的地块。光明与黑暗在音乐中相互渗透渗透，情绪流转不息。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 挪威Camilla Hole Trio的最新专辑延续前作将传统挪威民间音乐与即兴爵士融合的路线，相较于上一张偏向外太空科幻合成器探索的概念，本次回归更为质朴踏实的方向。主奏乐器高音萨克斯贯穿全作，挪威西部传统春之舞曲旋律被作为即兴素材重新解构。贝斯手与鼓手角色边界模糊，常相互交换旋律与节奏功能，叠加模块合成器与颤音琴增添音色层次。整张作品以集体即兴为核心手法，在保留民谣根脉的同时拓展至自由爵士的开放语汇，是北欧当代爵士跨界民间传统的一次沉稳尝试。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自挪威独立厂牌 Taragot 的北欧民间音乐跨界专辑，由一位瑞典小提琴家、两位挪威音乐家组成的三重奏演绎斯堪的纳维亚传统舞曲。专辑以挪威 Setesdal 山谷的小提琴曲开场，暗合水妖 Fossgrimen 的传说，暗示民间舞曲表面欢愉下隐藏的不安暗流。编曲上虽以传统舞蹈旋律为素材，却不用于伴舞，而是将器乐对话转化为室内乐式的亲密探讨。Tellef Kvifte 多以竖笛（sjøfløyte）担纲主奏旋律，同时引入萨克斯与风笛等挪威传统之外的乐器；Mats Edén 的小提琴与 Knut Kvifte Nesheim 的鼓组共同构建出模糊、即兴、碎片化的织体，旋律在齐奏与瓦解之间反复游走。专辑对传统素材进行了非正统的解构，揭示出北欧民间音乐中被忽略的内在复杂性。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家 Omar Sosa 在意大利 Fazioli 钢琴音乐厅完成了一次长达两小时的独奏即兴录音，作为专辑《Sendas》的基础素材。录制时值新冠封锁期间，他婚姻告终，在空旷的音乐厅中以 Fazioli 大钢琴进行无脚本的即兴演奏，后期加入人声采样、打击乐、loop、田野录音与多年来收集的环境声响，形成层次丰富的混合作品。Sosa 强调反对风格归类、追求首次录制的自然状态，并提及音乐应如喉音般触及低脉轮，与传统保持连结。专辑延续了他对禅意冥想与多元文化融合的探索，将非洲、古巴节奏元素与自由即兴结合。乐评聚焦创作过程与艺术哲学，对具体音乐细节描述有限，但展现了独立艺术家的创作理念与跨文化视野。

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评是对2026年8月实验音乐新作的综合性巡礼，由Marc Masters撰写。内容涵盖多种前沿声音实践：Bromp Treb的弹性噪音构建、Enneads的抽象钢琴三重奏、Etelin的模块合成器嗡鸣、Asha Sheshadri的言语类声响作品，以及Maia Urstad基于无线电信号的拼贴。Andrew Weathers的田野录音、Dsic的计算机音乐也在讨论范围内。文章本身偏向汇编性质而非深度评论，对每张作品仅提供简短定位，缺乏具体的声音描述或创作背景分析。作为信息索引具有一定参考价值，帮助听众快速了解当月实验音乐动态，但难以替代深入的乐评内容。

items.body: Review by Progfan97402 — Melange was a two album wonder out of Spain. Viento Bravo is their second album and their final one. While their debut is good it suffers from the usual double album filler syndrome towards the end. Viento Bravo has none of those issues. This one was released on the now-defunct Beyond Beyond is Beyond Records, this is the same label that gave us the wonderful Japanese Canterbury band De Loreans. This is one seriously retro album where they even recorded with authentic recording equipment and gear, sort of like those artists who recorded at Toe Rag Studios in London, but this was recorded in Madrid. How to describe this? It's clear there's a psychedelic vibe to it but the prog elements are there. It makes me think of Magick Brother and Mystic Sister but without the female vocals or Canterbury influence even though Melange predates that band. The vocals are all in Spanish. The album starts of with the truly wonderful "R�o Revuelto", a wonderful and lively number. It's amazing I'm hearing this and it's from 2017. "Cheroqui" looks like it's the Spanish spelling of the Native American tribe Cherokee although you won't find any Native American influences in the music, although I'm not sure about the lyrics as the album never had the printed lyrics and I don't know Spanish. "Cotard" has a bit of that Spanish/flamenco feel to it, it also has a bit of that Middle Eastern feel as well. "Armos Preparadas" is just an amazing piece that simply blows me away. "Splendor Solis" is the closing piece and the lengthiest. This one has a bit of that Santana-like Latin American feel to it where the music goes into precision overdrive and speeds up towards the end. This is truly one of the finest albums I have ever heard that absolutely no one talks about. The only thing likely preventing a wider audience is the language barrier but I have never let that get in the way. Truly an album not to be overlooked.

items._cn_summary: VERSA 乐队在 2022 年首作中曾邀请多位客座乐手，呈现经典前卫摇滚风格；而 2024 年的《A Voyage / A Destination Part 2》则大幅转向，仅保留一位合成器客座，整体呈现出后摇特有的悠长流动感。专辑将摇滚编制与古典器乐相融合，营造出忧郁冥想氛围，段落如水般自然过渡，并以漫长的梦幻渐强推动情绪发展。评论将其与 Explosions in the Sky、Sigur Rós 的意境氛围相类比，同时部分段落展现出 Big Big Train 式的英式田园气质，说明乐队在保持核心氛围的同时具备一定的音乐广度。相比首作，方向更鲜明、情绪更内敛，适合偏好氛围化器乐作品的听众。

items.body: I walk through fire with my head held high Is that really such a crime? Leaving a faith can redraw the borders of reality. Certainties that once governed time, guilt, desire, and the fate of the self fall away at once, leaving freedom inseparable from vertigo. A person must decide which pieces of the old world deserve burial, which can be carried forward, and how to inhabit a life no longer mapped by inherited answers. Portland post-punk quartet Nyx Division enters that exposed territory with By Design, a new single rooted in vocalist Domino Monet’s experience of escaping the Mormon church. Released ahead of the band’s East Coast dates, including a set at NYC’s A Murder of Crows, the song follows the collapse of a prescribed worldview into the frightening, sensuous freedom of choosing what comes next. Monet describes the subject as “the liminal expanse between awe and terror,” where ontological loss meets the exhilaration of reconstructing a world from its broken pieces. By Design opens with acoustic guitar and a dry, vibraslap-like rattle, setting a touch of spaghetti-Western theater ahead of Monet’s first lines. The full band soon bears down through Justin Cory’s heavy guitar figures and Mason Wilkinson’s firm percussion, while Alex Rivas sends a nimble bassline dancing underneath. As the initial force relaxes into a melodic groove, the track takes on a psychedelic hue. Cory’s guitar reaches toward the broad alt-rock and shoegaze sweep of bands like Catherine Wheel while retaining the core rhythmic pull of 80s post-punk. Monet supplies the song’s greatest sense of scale. Her held notes tremble with heat and conviction, drawing upon the commanding tradition of women rock singers from the 1970s and ’80s. Fire, memory, sin, and survival pass through the lyrics as lived conditions rather than decoration. The repeated title carries a productive reversal: language often used to justify a divinely ordered universe becomes a declaration of self-authorship. Design now belongs to the person who endured the old plan and walked away with the right to make another. That tension gives the track its lift. The music recognizes the cost of departure while making room for appetite, beauty, and volition. Its dance-floor momentum feels connected to the body’s return after years spent beneath doctrine, and its desert atmosphere suggests an open horizon where terror and possibility share the same immense sky. Listen to By Design below: By Design by Nyx Division Formed in Portland in 2021, Nyx Division brings post-punk, goth, and rock ’n’ roll into a muscular, romantic union. The group released the Dark Star EP in 2022, followed by the 2025 singles Soldier of Love and Midnight Lights. By Design expands that approach through acoustic color, psychedelic breadth, and a hard-earned sense of release. Nyx Division now heads across the East Coast for four early-September appearances. The band shares the Philadelphia, Worcester, and Cambridge dates with eX-Tradition. Their September 4 stop places them at New York’s Bowery Ballroom for the first of the festival’s two main nights at A Murder of Crows XI, appearing alongside Anja Huwe, Rosegarden Funeral Party, Creux Lies, and Guilty Strangers. items.album: New Zealand Post-Punk Outfit Trauma Party Confronts the Political Circus in Fiery Video for “Roll Up (It’s the New Truth)”

items.body: They’re bringing their violence They’re bringing their bile They’re juggling their words They’re bringing the new truth Trauma Party have found the right instrument for 2026: a busted carnival loudspeaker wired straight into the national nervous system. Roll Up (It’s the New Truth), the final video single drawn from the New Zealand group’s debut EP Because You’ve Been Good, barrels forward on rolling drums and blackened guitar, turning political disgust into a carnival bark that grows more feverish with every repetition. There is some of The Fall’s sour wit in the delivery, some Killing Joke in the pressure underneath, and a trace of Sham 69 in the gang-minded force of the refrain. Then the psychedelic stink rolls in. The Crazy World of Arthur Brown feels close at hand, while the guitars occasionally carry the broad, wounded sweep associated with The Chameleons. Trauma Party throws these ingredients into a garage-rock furnace and lets the song stagger around like a circus tent caught in a riot. The lyrics present authoritarian politics as cheap entertainment turned lethal. A fat orange clown presides over cages, bile, violence, snake oil, obedient freaks, and language mangled until falsehood becomes official reality. The joke keeps curdling because the circus imagery is funny for roughly half a second before its implications land. Spectacle becomes governance, repetition becomes persuasion, and the crowd is expected to applaud while vocabulary itself is dragged behind the tent and beaten senseless. “This song is not quiet; it screams at us all to wake up and beware ‘the new truth’ and the surreality of alternative facts,” the band says. “It’s a fiery post-punk alert from the fringes, illustrating the strength of art and music as tools of resistance.” Buddy Olson pushes the point further with a statement whose terse menace could have been painted across a barricade: “The privileged are few. We have them surrounded. Don’t let them escape. Hold them accountable.” The accompanying video gives the song an appropriately lawless setting. Filmed outside The Woolshed, Trauma Party’s clubhouse at the Waiheke Dirt Track, the band perform beneath a cold moon amid fire, smoke, and Molotov cocktails. Cars continue passing in the background, an almost comic detail that makes the scene more disturbing: apocalypse as roadside attraction, fury blazing a few metres away while ordinary traffic keeps moving, while everyone is expected to call the wreckage progress again. There is a Mad Max quality to the imagery, crossed with the scruffy end-times fatalism of A Boy and His Dog, yet the cheap-thrills destruction carries political purpose. Watch the video for Roll Up (It’s The New Truth) below: Trauma Party closes their EP Because You’ve Been Good by making the circus grotesque, psychedelic, and dangerously catchy. The tents are up, the clown is talking, the audience is already inside, and somewhere behind the music somebody is selling the lie as admission price. Listen to Roll Up (It’s The New Truth) below and order the single here. items._cn_summary: 新西兰乐队Trauma Party的首张EP《Because You've Been Good》以单曲《Roll Up (It's the New Truth)》收尾，将政治厌恶化为嘉年华式的叫卖。乐队以破碎的扩音器意象隐喻扭曲的公共话语系统，滚动的鼓点与黑化吉他构成压力的底色，歌词以笼中怪人、油腔滑调的政客形象呈现威权政治作为廉价娱乐的致命性。音乐融合The Fall式的尖刻、Killing Joke式的压迫、Sham 69式的合唱力量以及Arthur Brown式的迷幻气息，编曲粗粝而不失层次。MV拍摄于乐队的Waiheke Dirt Track俱乐部外，月光下火焰与烟雾交织，过往车辆的反日常细节强化了末日场景的荒诞感。整体呈现出一种介乎车库摇滚与迷幻后朋克之间的粗野美学，以嬉笑怒骂的方式回应现实政治。

items.album: Tomorrows Letters release ‘Up Against the Wall’, the first single from a debut album
items.excerpt: Minsk-based project Tomorrows Letters released the noir synthpop single “Up Against the Wall” on 31 August 2026, the first track lifted from the debut album Kiryl Karotki plans to issue this autumn. The self-released single runs to three versions on streaming services, the original at 3:46, an extended version at 4:26 and a 2:54 remix by the Belarusian post-punk band Nürnberg. The Bandcamp edition pairs the original with the extended version. Karotki records Tomorrows Letters alone.
items.body: Minsk-based project Tomorrows Letters released the noir synthpop single “Up Against the Wall” on 31 August 2026, the first track lifted from the debut album Kiryl Karotki plans to issue this autumn. The self-released single runs to three versions on streaming services, the original at 3:46, an extended version at 4:26 and a 2:54 remix by the Belarusian post-punk band Nürnberg. The Bandcamp edition pairs the original with the extended version. Karotki records Tomorrows Letters alone. Nürnberg’s sound engineer Andrei Bobrovka mixed and mastered the track, and Karotki produced the cover artwork. The three versions run to 11 minutes and 6 seconds in total, and the release is out on Bandcamp and Spotify. Up Against The Wall by Tomorrows Letters What Tomorrows Letters says about ‘Up Against the Wall’ The song stages an internal trial in which the accused and the judge are the same person. Karotki explains what the arrangement is built around before the lyric reaches its closing line, “I’m a prisoner of my own mind”: “The song describes a state where your own mind acts as both the prosecutor and the judge in a trial that never ends. It’s about being your own worst enemy, trapped in a loop of self-judgment where conscience acts as a punisher rather than a moral guide.” A saxophone-like drone opens the recording before a mechanised groove takes over. Sparse piano notes sit next to Karotki’s measured vocal, and trip-hop menace and industrial textures run through the rhythm alongside the darker electronic pop of Depeche Mode‘s 1990s and early-2000s records. The saxophone returns between verses, winding through organ-like keys and a low electronic buzz, and the clipped construction carries the same severity as 1980s minimal synth. The lyric keeps to the courtroom setting throughout. Past mistakes supply the testimony, the mirror holds the verdict, and the heartbeat keeps time for the fear. Inside what the song calls the courtroom of the soul, the singer takes every role and pays every toll, until the line between right and wrong turns into another form of captivity. The Nürnberg remix is the first of several guest appearances and collaborations Karotki has lined up for the album. About Tomorrows Letters Tomorrows Letters is the solo project of Kiryl Karotki, based in Minsk, Belarus. The project mixes minimal synth and New Romantic sources with trip-hop rhythm and industrial texture, and Karotki works to a hardware-only rule, building tracks on vintage samplers and drum machines rather than software. His writing returns to a fixed set of subjects: isolation, self-judgment, Jungian ideas about the hidden self, maladaptive daydreaming, compulsive creation, and victories that turn out to be empty once won. “Up Against the Wall” takes the second of those directly as its structure. The samplers and drum machines leave the recordings with a dusty, tactile surface. Karotki’s collaborators on the single come from the same city. Nürnberg, the Minsk post-punk band whose engineer Andrei Bobrovka mixed and mastered the track, also supplied the remix that closes the release. The project’s earlier releases, the singles “So Be It” and “Go For It”, went out the same way “Up Against the Wall” has, self-released through its own Bandcamp page and the streaming services rather than through a label. The three versions of the single split the material three ways. The original runs 3:46, the extended version stretches it to 4:26, and the Nürnberg remix cuts it back to 2:54 and carries a joint artist credit to Tomorrows Letters and Nürnberg rather than a remixer credit alone. “Up Against the Wall” opens the run-up to the debut Tomorrows Letters LP. No title, tracklist or release date has been announced for the album beyond the autumn 2026 window, and no further guest names have been confirmed.
items._cn_summary: 明斯克艺术家Kiryl Karotki以个人项目Tomorrows Letters发行单曲《Up Against the Wall》，这是其首张专辑的首支单曲。作品定位为黑色合成器流行，融入了trip-hop节奏与工业质感，并提到Depeche Mode九十年代及早期两千年代作品作为参照。制作严格遵循纯硬件路线，使用老式采样器与鼓机完成编曲，赋予录音一种颗粒感与触觉质地。音乐结构围绕一场内在审判展开，歌词以法庭意象构建自我审判的闭环，萨克斯般的嗡鸣、机械化律动、稀疏钢琴与低频电子蜂鸣交替出现于段落之间。Nürnberg乐队提供的混音版本作为客座合作延伸了作品的质感边界。整体呈现了一种克制而阴暗的氛围美学，以极简合成器骨架承载内省式的文本概念。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As soon as you start listening to Quickly Quickly Quickly, and their opening track, "Firebears", you are plunged into a sonic explosion you weren't prepared for; it is a surprise that stirs you in much the same way hearing classic 70s bands for the first time did. I was reminded of King Crimson, there is something epic about it, yet also dark and dangerous, and yet I also thought of Sonic Youth, who, incidentally, also feature two guitarists, a crucial element in creating that sonic canvas.The way the keyboards and guitars intertwine was also innovative, and that was nothing compared to what followed, as the McGowan brothers sing with such deep emotion and grit. This sets them apart from other bands that might be solid instrumentally but, at least to my ears, lack a distinctive signature. The arrangements constantly shift and adapt to the unfolding music, a progression that is hard to predict, with the vocals guiding the instruments as they collectively build the melody, reversing the usual dynamic.Contrasts emerge quickly; a more introspective section takes on a nearly jazzy feel, albeit indirectly, and the piano can be as laid-back as Neil Young during the moments when Crazy Horse was resting. Towards the end, at times I thought I heard the voice of Chris Cornell from Soundgarden, specifically during his band's psychedelic moments, and I found that same powerful vocal range, imbued with genuine emotion, once again in The Tea Club."The Eternal German Infant" presents a contrast between its instrumental power, a kind of restrained violence, and the vulnerability of the vocals; it then plunges into imagery woven from seemingly disjointed guitar, bass, and keyboard notes, with the guitar tearing at notes as if seeking a meeting point between the spirit of the voice and the music, a near-theatrical encounter."Mister Freeze" opens another door within the established framework, that dreamlike (or perhaps nightmarish) atmosphere, as if hundreds of crystal shards were parting to clear the way: an acoustic guitar paired with electric strumming that hangs like a curtain of stained glass catching the sunlight. The same notes repeat, yet with a certain decomposition, like fruit left too long in the summer sun. The subtlety of David Sylvian's solo work gains ground, casting a protective mantle, that sheltering sky spoken of by writer Paul Bowles, evoking a desert soundtrack: the organ, the strumming guitar... and one mask concealing another."I Shall Consume Everything" layers on intensity, steadily building tension; drums and a guitar join the keyboards, shifting from the style of the early Fripp (circa 1969) to the Greek echoes of Aphrodite's Child, until a guitar riff finally tears down what was built, driven by distortion, overlapping and repeating vocals, and rhythmic breaks that shatter the melody, causing it to quickly fade away......was any disintegration worthy of the name ever slow?
items._genre: crossover prog / progressive rock / experimental rock
items._cn_summary: The Tea Club的《Quickly Quickly Quickly》以双吉他配置构建了宽阔的声场，键盘与吉他的交织充满实验意味。McGowan兄弟的演唱被多次与Chris Cornell、David Sylvian相提并论，展现出从暴烈到内省的宽广情感光谱。专辑在编曲上不断变换走向，旋律由人声引导而非乐器，颠倒了常规动态关系。部分段落呈现接近爵士的内省质地，钢琴段落被比作Neil Young式的慵懒时光；其他曲目则具有梦魇般的氛围，分解的音符如同夏日暴晒下腐烂的水果。Aphrodite's Child式的希腊回响与早期Fripp的吉他风格被融入同一框架。整张专辑在器乐力量与人声脆弱感之间制造持续张力，尾曲以失真吉他和重复人声撕裂既有结构，让旋律迅速瓦解。

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — "Have one on Me" appeared 4 years after the landmark "Ys", with part of the delay relating to nodules on the singer's vocal cords in 2009 induced no doubt in part by her untrained and untamed pipes. Perhaps in reaction to her improved health and in an attempt not to repeat the same mistakes too quickly, this triple album of 3 LP length parts highlights more instrumental acumen, that is to say, it actually has breaks where she rests her voice, and some are the highlights of their respective tracks, indeed sometimes the only redeeming feature on the likes of "Good Intentions Paving Co". Joanna also sings in a more classically skilled manner without abandoning that whimsy entirely, even piling vocalise on the aforementioned and the title cut. These modifications coincide with and even steer the production into rock and jazz realms in preference to the chambered directives of the pre nodular Joanna. Merged with a handful of her best tunes- "'81", "Baby Birch", "On a Good Day", "In California", "Go Long" and "Kingfisher" - it's worth toasting (along with her health) if not wholeheartedly lionizing.
items._cn_summary: 这张三碟套装在作者嗓音结节康复后发行，相较前作大幅减少纯人声驱动的写法，腾出大量段落交由器乐主导，因而在'Good Intentions Paving Co'等曲目里出现全曲最出色的器乐间奏。作者声乐技巧趋于古典化，却未丢掉原有怪趣气息，并在标题曲中叠加密集花腔。整体制作方向由室内乐编排转向摇滚与爵士的交汇，曲目中包含'81'、'Baby Birch'、'On a Good Day'、'In California'、'Go Long'、'Kingfisher'等旋律上乘之作，构成一部兼具作者性与器乐探索的民谣长篇。
